  11. pod
  12. payment API

The problem

At 19:00 Nadia had a theory, and she liked it more than she should have. Two things with the same address. She had seen it once in Ruth's cupboard, two printers that had both been typed 192.168.1.20 by two different people, each answering to the name whenever it felt like it. Half the print jobs vanished. It had looked, she remembered, exactly like a third of everything failing.

"An address clash," she said. "Something old at 10.20.4.31, something new at 10.20.4.31, and the pods get whichever answers first."

Sam, passing with a sandwich, said that sounded very plausible, which was what Sam said about theories he could not check.

"Then find both of them," said Ruth.

Nadia searched the cloud console for the address. Not a machine, not a pod. A network interface, the cloud's name for one card in one machine with one address painted on it. And not one: three, one in each availability zone, all born at the same minute.

eni-0a9f3c   10.20.4.31   endpoints-a   created 15:58   VPC Endpoint Interface
eni-07d21e   10.20.5.31   endpoints-b   created 15:58   VPC Endpoint Interface
eni-0b44a7   10.20.6.31   endpoints-c   created 15:58   VPC Endpoint Interface

Every button on the page was greyed out. The interfaces belonged to something that lived in the platform account, where Jonas worked and Nadia did not have a login. But she could read them, and there was no fourth line. Nothing else in the VPC claimed 10.20.4.31. The address had exactly one owner, and the owner was eleven days younger than her notebook.

"Not a clash," she said, and crossed it out, which felt worse than it should have.

"Good," said Ruth. "Now. When your laptop wants to send something to 10.0.1.1, how does it know which van to put it in?"

◷Back then

Harold was there for the question before Ruth was. In 1982 his department had put in an Ethernet, the shared cable from chapter 6, and every machine on it had two addresses: the Ethernet address burned into its card, and the internet address someone had typed into a configuration file. The cable only understood the first. So each machine had to be told, by hand, the Ethernet address of every other machine it might want to talk to. Harold kept the table on a sheet of paper taped above the console, and every time a card was replaced the sheet was wrong.

David Plummer's answer, RFC 826 in November 1982, was that nobody should keep the table at all. When a machine needed the hardware address for 10.1.0.4, it would shout the question down the cable to everyone, and whichever machine owned that address would answer. The asker would remember the answer for a while and then forget it. The sheet of paper came down.

The second question, who decides what your address is in the first place, took ten more years. Ruth met it at the ISP in 1993, when business customers began turning up with laptops. Every address in the office was typed in by hand from a spreadsheet, and one afternoon a visiting salesman typed in the address of the office router, because it was the one he could see on a label, and took the whole floor off the internet until someone found him. There had been a scheme since 1985 called BOOTP for giving diskless workstations an address at boot, but it needed a table too. In October 1993 Ralph Droms published RFC 1531, DHCP, building on it: a machine joining the network asks for an address, a server lends it one for a fixed time, and the machine must come back to renew it or lose it. The spreadsheet went in a drawer, Ruth said, and stayed there.

The idea

A machine that has only now been plugged in knows nothing. It has to answer three questions before it can send a single packet anywhere useful: what is my address, how do I reach the machine next to me, and where do I send everything else.

DHCP, the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol, answers the first. It is the council assigning a house number when you move in. The new machine has no address, so it broadcasts to everyone on its street, and a DHCP server replies with an offer. The exchange has four steps, and engineers remember them by their initials.

The answer is a lease: the address is lent, not given, for a fixed time, and the machine must renew it or lose it. With the address comes the subnet mask from the last chapter, the address of a gateway, and the address of a name server. In a cloud, the DHCP server is not a machine you can find; the estate itself answers, and the lease is for whatever the interface has been assigned.

ARP, the Address Resolution Protocol, answers the second question. The machine now knows that 10.0.1.1 is on its own street, but the street, the Ethernet from chapter 6, only delivers to MAC addresses, the name painted on the van. So the machine shouts down the corridor: who lives at number 1? The owner answers, and the asker keeps the answer in its ARP cache for a few minutes.

The third question is answered by one line of configuration. The default gateway is the address on your own street to which you send everything that is not on your own street. It is the sign in the post room that says "everything else goes to the main sorting office". The machine ARPs for the gateway's MAC address once, and from then on every packet for another network goes into a frame addressed to the gateway, with the real destination still written inside the envelope. The gateway is a router, and chapter 12 is about what it does next.

Two details matter in a cloud. First, nobody shouts on a real wire. The host that runs your virtual machine answers the ARP question itself, from a table of every interface in the estate, and it will not relay an answer from anyone else. Second, an address does not belong to a machine. It belongs to a network interface, the cloud's record of one card with one MAC address and one or more IP addresses, in one subnet. An interface can be attached to a virtual machine, or to a managed service that has no machine you will ever see. The estate knows exactly where each interface is, and it delivers to the interface, not to whatever is behind it.

Remember it as: DHCP gives you a house number, ARP finds the van for your own street, and the default gateway takes everything else.

That was why there could be no clash. 10.20.4.31 was one interface, in one subnet, created at 15:58, and the estate delivered to it without ever asking who lived there. Nadia's pods were sending their packets to the right door; the door was new.

⚠Where it breaks
  • ARP spoofing attack: a machine on the subnet answers "the gateway is at my MAC address" before the real gateway does, and every packet for the outside world passes through it first. The sign is the gateway's MAC address changing in the ARP cache, or a cache entry that disagrees with the switch. Switches that check ARP replies against the DHCP record stop it, and a cloud host that answers ARP itself never forwards the lie.
  • Rogue DHCP server attack: a box someone plugged in answers Discover faster than the real server and hands out its own address as the gateway. The sign is machines with addresses from a range nobody recognises, working for a while and then not. Switches that allow DHCP replies only from a known port stop it; in a cloud the estate is the only server.
  • Duplicate address: two machines are typed the same address, and each answers ARP for it in turn. The sign is connectivity that comes and goes with no pattern, and an ARP cache that flips between two MAC addresses. Leases instead of typing, and a machine that checks whether its new address is already in use before it keeps it, prevent it.

…but

So nothing was fighting over 10.20.4.31. It had one owner, born at 15:58, and the only wrong thing about it was that a pod asking for api.paystream.example was sent there at all. Something was doing the sending.

Chapter 11 · Act IIIIt's Always DNS#

  1. the wire
  2. phone
  3. Wi-Fi
  4. ISP
  5. internet
  6. DNS
  7. CDN edge
  8. load balancer
  9. VPC
  10. node
  11. pod
  12. payment API

The problem

At 19:30 Sam typed "it's always DNS" for the third time, and this time Nadia did not roll her eyes, because she was starting to think he was half right.

Something was telling the pods that api.paystream.example lived at 10.20.4.31. Pods do not invent addresses. They ask. So she asked the same question again from a node, and this time she read the whole answer instead of the short one.

;; ANSWER SECTION:
api.paystream.example.   60   IN   A   10.20.4.31
;; SERVER: 10.0.0.2

Two things she had never looked at before. The answer had come from 10.0.0.2, an address at the very bottom of Kettle's own block, which meant the directory being consulted was inside the VPC. And the 60 meant the answer was only good for a minute. She had read somewhere that the payment client library kept addresses for five minutes regardless. She wrote 60 s vs 5 min and underlined it.

Then she asked a different directory. From the same node she sent the question to a public resolver on the internet instead of the one the node had been given.

$ dig +short @1.1.1.1 api.paystream.example
203.0.113.10

"Same name," she said. "Two phone books. Ours says ten twenty. Everyone else's says the real one."

"Which one is lying?" said Ruth.

"Neither. That's the problem. Ours was told to say it."

Ruth nodded as if that were the first properly interesting thing anyone had said all evening. "Then it isn't DNS that's broken. DNS is doing exactly what someone asked it to do at two minutes to four."

◷Back then

Ruth's first boss, Harold, had kept a printed copy of a file called HOSTS.TXT in his desk drawer, and in 1983 he was still updating it by hand. Every machine on the network had a line in that file: a name, an address. When a new machine joined, you downloaded the new file from a computer at Stanford. By the early eighties the file was being fetched so often that fetching it was a noticeable share of the network's traffic, and names had started to collide, because two sites would each want to call their machine "mail".

Paul Mockapetris was asked to find a way out. His answer, published as RFC 882 and 883 in November 1983, was to stop having one file at all. Names would be a tree. The root knew who was responsible for com and edu and uk; those knew who was responsible for the names beneath them; and so on down. Nobody held the whole list. Each organisation held its own branch and answered questions about it. He called it the Domain Name System, and Harold, Ruth said, had grumbled for a year that it would never catch on, because who would run the root.

Twenty-five years later Ruth was running a data centre, and in July 2008 she spent a weekend patching every resolver in it. Dan Kaminsky, a security researcher, had found that the small random number a resolver uses to match an answer to its question could be guessed, and that an attacker who asked a resolver for thousands of made-up names in a row could slip in a forged answer for a real one, and poison the resolver's memory for as long as it chose. He kept the details back for a month so that every vendor could ship a fix on the same day. The fix was to make the resolver's question harder to guess by sending it from a random port as well. "Everybody patched," Ruth said, "and then everybody checked whether they had actually patched, which is a different thing."

The idea

DNS is the phone book of the network, except that nobody prints it. It turns a name people can remember, api.paystream.example, into an address packets can use. When a machine needs that address, it does not go looking itself. It asks a recursive resolver, a server run by its network or its cloud whose job is to do the walking, and the resolver asks a chain of other servers in turn.

The chain follows the tree. At the top are the root servers, which know only who is responsible for each top-level domain, the last label in a name: com, uk, example. The top-level domain's servers know who is responsible for each name beneath them. At the bottom is the authoritative server for paystream.example, run by Paystream or its DNS provider, which holds the actual records and gives the final answer.

Each answer is a record, and records come in types. The ones an engineer meets most often fit in one table.

Type Holds Example
A an IPv4 address api.paystream.example is 203.0.113.10
AAAA an IPv6 address, four times as long the same name on the newer internet
CNAME another name to look up instead shop.kettle.example is really d1x.cdn.example
MX where email for the domain should go kettle.example mail goes to mail.kettle.example
TXT free text, used for proving you own a name "this domain is verified by…"

Every record comes with a TTL, time to live, a number of seconds the resolver may remember the answer for before it must ask again. Caching is why DNS is fast and why it is confusing. The resolver remembers; the operating system remembers; often the application remembers too, for a time of its own choosing that has nothing to do with the TTL. A record changed at 15:58 reaches a machine that asked at 15:57 one minute later, a machine whose client library caches for five minutes at 16:03, and a machine holding an answer it will not re-check until it restarts never.

A resolver inside a cloud network can be told to answer a public name with a private address. That is called split-horizon DNS: the same name gives one answer from inside the estate and another from outside. Clouds sell it as a private DNS zone, a private phone book that overrides the public one for anyone who asks from within the VPC. It is not a fault. It is a feature, and it is what Friday's change switched on.

Two words to recognise for later. DNSSEC adds signatures to records so a resolver can tell a forged answer from a real one. Encrypted DNS carries the question itself inside an encrypted connection so that nobody on the path can read or change it. Neither was in play at Kettle, and neither would have helped: the private answer was signed by nobody and intended by somebody.

Remember it as: DNS is directory enquiries with a memory: the answer you get depends on who you ask and how long ago they last asked.

So Sam was half right. It was DNS in the sense that DNS was handing out a new address, and not DNS in the sense that DNS was obeying. The caches explain the shape of the failure too: pods drifted onto the new answer one at a time as their caches expired, a third at first, more as the evening went on, until the 17:30 restart emptied every cache at once.

⚠Where it breaks
  • DNS cache poisoning attack: an attacker guesses the transaction number and slips a false answer into a resolver's cache. The sign is a name that resolves somewhere strange for exactly one TTL, then recovers. Random source ports and DNSSEC stop it, and the browser's padlock check limits the damage.
  • Stale DNS cache: a record changes, but some resolvers and some application libraries keep the old answer. The sign is a change that "works for some people" and a failure rate that creeps instead of jumping. Lower the TTL before a change, and know what your client library caches on its own.
  • Hijack of the registration attack: nobody poisons anything; they log in to the registrar and change the records. The sign is a padlock warning from a site that was fine yesterday, and an authoritative answer that is wrong. Lock the registrar account with strong authentication and a registry lock.
  • Testing from the wrong horizon: a name is checked from a laptop, where it resolves to the public address, and declared fine. The sign is "works for me" from everyone outside the estate. Test from where the traffic comes from.

…but

DNS had done what it was told: inside the estate, send Paystream's name to 10.20.4.31. The pods were obeying, and their packets were leaving with the right address on the front. Whether they could get there was a question for the sorting office.

The problem

At 20:00 the office had emptied to the three of them and the hum of the fridge. Sam had gone to sit with the CEO. Nadia had the packets leaving the pods with 10.20.4.31 on the front, and she had the interface at the far end. What she did not have was the road between.

"If the address is in a different district," she said, "then something has to carry it there. A gateway. Which means a route."

"Then read the routes," said Ruth.

The cloud console had a page for it. Every subnet in the VPC was attached to a route table, a short list of where packets for each destination should go. Nadia opened the one for the node subnets.

Destination       Target
10.0.0.0/16       local
10.20.0.0/16      local
0.0.0.0/0         nat-0c71e2

There was one more line, between the second and the last. She did not read it, because it was not what she was looking for. What she was looking for was there: 10.20.0.0/16, target local. The estate would carry it itself. No gateway, no box in the middle, nothing to blame.

To be sure, she went back to the debug pod and traced the road.

$ traceroute -n 10.20.4.31
 1  * * *
 2  * * *

"Stars," she said. "No hops at all. Not even one."

"Local means the estate delivers it by hand," said Ruth. "One street to the next, no sorting office between. The stars are the other end not answering, which we already knew. Routing takes the letter to the door, Nadia. It doesn't make anybody open it."

Nadia wrote routing: fine and, after a moment, annoyingly.

◷Back then

In 1995 the ISP in Reading had two big routers in a cage, and every road out of the building was typed into them by hand. A customer's block went in as one line: this prefix, that next hop. Ruth had typed hundreds of those lines, and she remembered one of them better than the rest, because she had typed the mask wrong. A customer's /24 went in as a /16, and for an hour every packet for a hundred other customers' networks was quietly carried to one small firm's leased line, which dropped them on the floor. Nothing alarmed. Nothing broke that a dashboard could see. The phone rang, and kept ringing.

Static routes, she said, were fine when you had ten of them and poison when you had a thousand. The alternative was to let the routers work the map out for themselves. The oldest way was a protocol called RIP, in which each router told its neighbours every few seconds how many hops away it thought every network was, and the neighbours believed it. It was simple and it was slow; news of a dead link crawled across the network one hop at a time, and for minutes routers would happily send packets down a road that no longer existed.

The ISP moved to OSPF the year after the bad mask. Instead of passing rumours about distances, every router described its own links to every other router, so each one held the same complete map and computed the shortest path itself. When a link died, the router that noticed told everyone at once, and within seconds every router had redrawn the map. "You stop typing roads," Ruth said, "and start describing the ground. The roads follow." Harold, she added, had watched the first version of this on ARPANET, where the IMPs from chapter 3 had done something of the sort among themselves long before anyone outside the network had to care.

The idea

A router is a machine with more than one street, whose only job is to take a packet from one and hand it to the next on the way to its destination. It is the sorting office. It does not read the letter and it does not care who sent it. It reads the postcode on the front and puts the letter in a pigeonhole.

The pigeonholes are the routing table, a list of rows, each with a destination prefix and a next hop. The next hop is either an interface, meaning "this street, deliver it directly", or the address of another router on one of its streets, meaning "hand it to them". Rows are written as CIDR blocks from chapter 9, and a packet's destination may match more than one.

That is where the one rule of routing comes in. A router chooses the row with the longest prefix match: among all the rows whose block contains the destination, the one with the most network bits wins, because it is the most specific. A /24 beats a /16, which beats a /8, which beats the last row of all.

The last row is the default route, 0.0.0.0/0, which matches every address and wins only when nothing else does. It is "everything else goes to the main sorting office". On a laptop it points at the home router. In Kettle's VPC it points at the NAT gateway, the machine that carries traffic out to the internet, which chapter 14 explains. The word local in a cloud route table means the estate itself is the next hop: every subnet in the VPC can reach every other, and the cloud's fabric delivers the packet without a router you can see.

Routing is hop by hop. No router knows the whole road. Each one chooses only the next office and trusts that office to choose the one after, which is why two routers that each think the other is the way forward can pass a packet between them for ever. To stop the for ever, every packet carries a TTL, a counter that starts at some number like 64 and goes down by one at each router. When it reaches zero the router drops the packet and sends a small message back to the sender saying time exceeded, and from where.

That small message is the whole trick of traceroute. It sends a packet with a TTL of 1 and notes who complained. Then a TTL of 2, and a TTL of 3, until the destination itself answers. Each complaint names one router on the road.

A row of stars means nobody complained at that distance. The router may be configured not to answer, or there may be no router there at all, because the estate delivers locally and the far end is silent.

Routes get into tables in two ways. A static route is typed by a person and never changes. A dynamic route is learned from a routing protocol, in which routers tell each other what they can reach. Inside one organisation the protocols are called interior: RIP, which counts hops and is rarely used now, and OSPF, in which every router shares a map of its links and computes the shortest paths itself. A cloud route table is static, written by whoever owns the VPC, and the local rows are written by the cloud and cannot be removed.

Remember it as: a router reads only the postcode, picks the most specific pigeonhole, and hands the letter one office on.

Kettle's table had a row for 10.20.0.0/16, it was the longest match, and it said local. The road to the new door was short, straight and correctly signed, which meant the thing that was dropping the packets was not on the road.

⚠Where it breaks
  • Asymmetric routing: the outbound packet takes one road and the reply takes another, so a box in the middle that keeps state, a firewall or a NAT, sees only half the conversation and drops the half it does not understand. The sign is SYN leaving, a reply visible on a different link, and nothing arriving. Make both roads pass the same box, or make the box stateless.
  • Black hole from a wrong static route: a typed row with the wrong mask or next hop swallows traffic for a block that was never meant to be there. The sign is traffic for many destinations vanishing after one small change, with no error from anything. Review routes as carefully as code, and prefer learned routes to typed ones.
  • Routing loop: two routers each believe the other is the way forward. The sign is traceroute showing the same pair of addresses alternating until the TTL runs out. Protocols that share a full map, like OSPF, converge out of it; static routes do not.

…but

The estate carried the letter to the door. Before Friday, it had carried the same letter a great deal further: out of the building, across the city and back in. Nadia wanted to see that old road.

The problem

At 20:30 Nadia did something she had not done all evening: she sent a packet to the address that used to work. Not the name, which the VPC's phone book would turn into 10.20.4.31, but Paystream's public address itself, straight from the debug pod.

$ traceroute -n 203.0.113.10
 1  * * *
 4  198.51.100.7    1.1 ms
 9  203.0.113.10    7.4 ms

Nine hops. One of them, at hop 4, was the NAT gateway's public address, the door the estate used to send things into the world. After that the road went somewhere she had never looked: a handful of routers with addresses that belonged to the cloud provider, then one that did not, then Paystream. And Paystream answered. The old road still existed. Nobody had closed it. Jonas had built a shorter one beside it and moved the signpost.

She wanted to know whose the middle routers were. Ruth showed her where to ask: a public register of who announces which blocks of addresses to the rest of the internet.

$ whois -h whois.radb.net 203.0.113.10
route:    203.0.113.0/24
origin:   AS64500
descr:    Paystream Ltd

"AS," said Nadia. "Autonomous system?"

"A country, roughly," said Ruth. "With its own post office. The cloud is one. Paystream's hosting is another. Before Friday your checkout letters left one country, crossed at least one more, and came back. Now they never leave the estate. The internet never saw tonight's packets, Nadia. Whatever is wrong with them, it's wrong inside your fence."

Nadia wrote old road: out and back. New road: never leaves. It was, she thought, the first thing all evening that made the change sound like an improvement.

◷Back then

Ruth had been told the beginning of this story so often that she told it as if she had been there. In June 1989 Kirk Lougheed of Cisco and Yakov Rekhter of IBM published RFC 1105, the first version of the Border Gateway Protocol. The interior protocols from the last chapter assumed one organisation, one map and one idea of a shortest path. The internet was becoming many organisations that did not share any of those. BGP let each network announce to its neighbours the blocks of addresses it could reach, with the list of networks the announcement had already passed through, and let each neighbour decide for itself which announcements to believe and pass on. It assumed goodwill, because in 1989 the people running the networks all knew each other.

Ruth saw what that assumption cost on a Sunday afternoon in February 2008. Pakistan Telecom had been ordered to block YouTube inside Pakistan, and did it by announcing a small, specific block of YouTube's addresses as its own, so that its customers' traffic would fall into a hole. Its upstream provider passed the announcement to the world. Because a more specific block always wins, routers everywhere believed Pakistan Telecom was the best road to YouTube, and for a good part of that afternoon it was unreachable from most of the planet. Nobody had broken in. One network had said something untrue, and every other network had believed it.

The other story she told Nadia was more recent, and Nadia half remembered it herself. On 4 October 2021 a configuration change inside Facebook withdrew the BGP announcements for the blocks that held its own DNS servers. Within minutes the rest of the internet had no road to the name servers, so no road to the names, so no road to anything. The outage lasted most of the working day, and the company's engineers were reported to have had trouble getting into their own buildings, because the door systems needed the network too. "The map didn't lie that time," Ruth said. "They erased themselves from it."

The idea

Inside one organisation, routers share a map and agree on the shortest path. The internet is not one organisation. It is tens of thousands of networks, each run by a company, a university, a cloud or a government, each with its own routers and its own rules. Each of those is an autonomous system, an AS, identified by a number, and the question of how a packet crosses from one to the next is the question of how the internet exists at all.

The answer is BGP, the Border Gateway Protocol. A router at the edge of each AS keeps a session with a router at the edge of each neighbouring AS. Over that session it announces the address blocks it can deliver to, and with each block the AS path, the list of AS numbers the announcement has passed through on its way. A neighbour that hears the same block from two directions prefers, all else being equal, the shorter path. Then it adds its own number and passes the announcement on. The picture a router ends up with is not a map of the internet. It is a list of blocks and, for each, the best next-door neighbour to hand it to.

Neighbours come in two kinds, and the difference is money. Transit is a service: a smaller network pays a larger one to carry its traffic to the whole internet and announce its blocks to everyone. Peering is an agreement between two networks to exchange traffic between their own customers directly, usually for free, because both save on transit. Much of that peering happens at an internet exchange, a building where many networks plug into one shared switch and can peer with each other over it. It is the postal treaty: countries agree which of each other's mail they will carry, and on what terms.

Two rules from chapter 12 still hold out here, and both have teeth. Routing is hop by hop, so no AS controls the road beyond its own border. And the longest prefix wins, so an AS that announces a more specific block than the real owner takes the traffic, whatever its path length. BGP has no way of checking that the network announcing a block is allowed to. It was built on trust, and it still mostly runs on it.

The repair, slowly spreading, is RPKI, a signed statement from the registry that owns a block saying which AS may announce it. A router that checks these statements can drop announcements that fail. Many large networks now check. Many do not. The map of the internet is still a thing nobody owns, assembled every minute from what each network tells the next.

A cloud customer is not an AS. The cloud provider is, and it speaks to the world on behalf of every VPC inside it. A packet from a pod to the public internet leaves the estate through the NAT gateway, is announced to the world under the provider's AS number, and comes back the same way.

Remember it as: BGP is countries' post offices telling each other which addresses they can reach, and believing each other.

That was the old road for Kettle's checkout: out through the cloud's AS, across an exchange or a transit link to Paystream's AS, and back. The new road did not cross a single border, so nothing on the internet could be at fault, and nothing on it could help.

⚠Where it breaks
  • Route leak or BGP hijack attack: a network announces a block it does not own, by mistake or on purpose, and because the more specific prefix wins, the world sends that block's traffic to it. The sign is a destination suddenly reachable only through a strange AS path, or not at all, while its own network is fine. RPKI checks at the receiving routers and limits on what each neighbour may announce stop most of it.
  • Withdrawn routes: a configuration change removes an organisation's own announcements, and the rest of the internet forgets how to reach it within minutes. The sign is a site that vanishes completely, DNS and all, rather than failing slowly. Keep the tools that fix the network reachable by a road the network does not control.
  • Trusting the shortest path: a route is chosen because its AS path is short, not because it is fast, and traffic between two cities crosses a continent. The sign is latency that does not match the geography. Networks tune their preferences by hand, and peering at a local exchange keeps local traffic local.

…but

If the new road was so short and so private, why had Jonas built it at all? The old one still worked. Nadia went back to the pull request and, this time, read the description instead of the title.

The problem

At 21:00 Nadia read the pull request properly, and found that Jonas had written four careful lines that nobody in the channel had quoted.

Why: during the September sale the NAT gateway hit ErrorPortAllocation
(peak 1,900/min) and checkouts failed for 20 min. NAT data processing is
also our largest network bill. Move Paystream to a private endpoint, no NAT.
Tested from node ip-10-0-1-42: curl https://api.paystream.example -> 200

She remembered the September sale: a sharp tooth in the error rate at the busiest ten minutes of the year, and a post-mortem with the words port allocation in it that she had not understood and had not asked about. Jonas had understood it. He had fixed it, on a Friday, and tested the fix.

"He tested it," she said. "From a node. It worked."

"From a node," said Ruth, and let it sit there. "Tell me what the NAT gateway does."

"It... lets the pods reach the internet. They've got private addresses, so it swaps them for a public one on the way out."

"One public one. For how many pods?"

"Forty-one. More in a sale. Each one opening connections."

"And how many desks does a post room have?"

Nadia looked at the word port in the pull request and felt it change meaning. Then Ruth said the other thing, the one Nadia wrote down without yet knowing why it mattered.

"Something else. On the old road, whatever address a pod had, Paystream never saw it. It saw the post room's address. The gateway's. That's gone now. Whoever's standing at the new door is seeing the pods as they really are, for the first time."

◷Back then

The number that had sounded infinite in 1981 stopped sounding infinite about a decade later, and Ruth spent the nineties watching the engineering of the internet rearrange itself around that fact.

The first patch came in May 1994. Kjeld Egevang and Paul Francis published RFC 1631, which described a box that would sit at the edge of a network and rewrite addresses as packets passed through it, so that a whole office could share a handful of public addresses, or one. They called it Network Address Translation and were careful to say it was a short-term fix, to buy time while something better was built. Ruth's ISP put its first business customers behind one that year, and the customers, who paid per address, were delighted.

The something better arrived on paper in December 1995. Steve Deering and Robert Hinden published RFC 1883, IPv6, with addresses of 128 bits, enough for every grain of sand to have a block of its own. Two months later, in February 1996, RFC 1918 set aside three address ranges that would never be routed on the public internet, so that everyone behind a NAT could use the same inside numbers without asking anyone. "They were meant to be the stopgap and the cure," Ruth said. "The stopgap won."

She was running a data centre by 3 February 2011, the day IANA, the registry at the top of the tree, handed out its last five large blocks to the regional registries and announced that the central pool was empty. The regional pools emptied over the following years. The price of a public address went up. ISPs that could not get more began putting whole towns of customers behind one translator, so that a home router was already translating, and then the carrier translated again. The short-term fix was seventeen years old and had become the shape of the internet.

The idea

IPv4 has about four billion addresses, and the world has far more than four billion things that want one. The early allocations were generous, whole class A blocks to single organisations, and by the mid-nineties it was clear the pool would exhaust. Two answers were designed at once: a bigger pool, and a way to share the pool you had. The second is the one almost every engineer lives behind today.

RFC 1918 defines three private address ranges. Addresses in them are never announced on the public internet, so any organisation may use them inside its own network, and millions do, all using the same numbers.

Range Prefix Addresses
10.0.0.0 to 10.255.255.255 10.0.0.0/8 16,777,216
172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255 172.16.0.0/12 1,048,576
192.168.0.0 to 192.168.255.255 192.168.0.0/16 65,536

A machine with a private address can send a packet to the public internet, but nobody out there can send one back, because no router outside knows a road to 10.0.1.42. NAT, Network Address Translation, is the box at the edge that solves this. It is the company post room: one public address on the building, and inside it a table of which desk each letter belongs to.

Sharing one public address among many machines needs more than swapping the address. Two pods may both open a connection to Paystream at the same moment, and the replies must find their way back to the right one. So the translator rewrites the source port too, the flat number from chapter 7, and keeps a row for each connection. This is port translation, and it is what nearly every NAT does.

The table is the limit. A port number is sixteen bits, so one public address has at most 65,536 ports, and in practice a translator keeps perhaps 55,000 of them for use. Each open connection from inside to the same outside address and port needs a row of its own. During a sale, hundreds of pods each opening dozens of connections to one payment API can use every row, and the next connection has nowhere to go. The gateway reports an error that engineers see as port allocation failed and customers see as a spinner. That is port exhaustion, and it was Jonas's September.

Two side effects of NAT matter as much as the thing itself. The first is that it hides the inside. Paystream's logs for the old road showed one address, the gateway's, for every pod at Kettle, because that is the only address that ever left the building. The second is that it blocks unsolicited inbound traffic, since a packet arriving from outside with no row in the table has no desk to go to and is dropped. This is NAT as accidental security: real protection, by accident, which people mistake for a firewall.

When the carrier runs out of public addresses too, it puts its customers' NAT boxes behind another one. This is carrier-grade NAT: a home router translates to a middle address, and the carrier's translator turns that into a public one. The middle layer needs addresses that are neither private, because customers already use those inside their homes, nor public, so a separate range was set aside for it, 100.64.0.0/10. Ruth said it turned up in the oddest places, which Nadia wrote down without asking why.

The bigger pool exists. IPv6 addresses are 128 bits long, written in hexadecimal with colons, like 2001:db8::1, and there are enough that nobody needs to share one. Adoption is slow for a plain reason: NAT works well enough, and IPv6 only helps once both ends and every road between speak it, which is the flag-day problem from chapter 8 spread across the whole planet. Most networks now run both, and most traffic still arrives over the old one.

Remember it as: NAT is the company post room: one public address outside, desk numbers inside, and a finite number of pigeonholes.

Friday's change took NAT out of the road to Paystream, which was the right cure for port exhaustion and for the bill. It also meant that, for the first time, the thing at the far end of the road saw each pod's own address instead of the post room's.

⚠Where it breaks
  • NAT port exhaustion: too many connections from inside to one outside destination use every port on the public address, and new ones fail. The sign is errors at the gateway that mention port allocation, at exactly the busiest moment. Add public addresses to the gateway, reuse connections instead of opening new ones, or take NAT out of the road.
  • NAT is not a firewall: it drops unsolicited inbound packets as a side effect, so people stop writing rules. The sign is a network with no deny rules anywhere and a comment saying "it's behind NAT". Write the rules anyway, and expect them to matter the day NAT is removed.
  • NAT hides the sender: every machine inside appears as one address outside, so the far end's logs, rate limits and allow lists all treat them as one. The sign is a whole office blocked because one laptop misbehaved, or logs that cannot say which pod made a request. Carry identity in the request itself, and remember that removing NAT reveals addresses the far end has never seen.

…but

Jonas had taken the post room out of the road for a good reason, and the new road was short, private and silent. A letter that arrives and is neither answered nor refused smells like a guard with a list. But the private letterbox had been installed from the platform account, and Nadia's badge did not open that door.

The problem

By 22:00 the office was down to two people and the hum of the fridge. Nadia's notebook had a page headed What we know, and the list had stopped growing an hour ago. Inside a pod the name went to 10.20.4.31. The route to it was local. Jonas had built the endpoint to stop paying the NAT gateway. A SYN left the pod and nothing came back.

Ruth had the capture from the debug pod open again. "Nothing," she said. "Not a reset. Not an error note from a router. A machine that is switched off gives you this. So does a machine that is on and has decided not to speak to you."

"A firewall."

"Something with a list. What do you have in your account that has a list?"

"Nothing called a firewall. I'd have seen it."

"You'd have seen a box with firewall written on it. That is not the same thing."

Nadia went back to the interface she had found on Friday evening. She could still see it. What she could not see was anything attached to it.

$ cloud network-interface list --filter address=10.20.4.31
10.20.4.31  eni-0a9f3c  endpoints-a  owner=platform-shared  rules: (no access)

"Platform-shared," Nadia read. "That's Jonas's account. The one with the endpoints and the shared subnets. I've got no role in it."

"Who grants one?"

"Jonas. Or Sam, for read-only, and Sam's been on the phone to the CEO since seven."

"Then ask Sam in the morning." Ruth stood and picked up her mug. "The thing you need to look at is behind a door you can't open tonight. Write down the question you would ask it, and go home."

Nadia wrote: Is there a guard on 10.20.4.31, and what is on its list? She underlined list, closed the notebook and went to find her coat.

◷Back then

Harold had been running a university machine on the night of 2 November 1988, Ruth said, and he liked to tell it as the night the internet grew up.

The thing arrived after dark, American time. It was a small program written by Robert Tappan Morris, a graduate student at Cornell, and it did what no program on the network had done before: it looked for other machines, broke in, copied itself across, and started looking again. It got in through holes that people already knew about and had not fixed: a debugging option left on in the mail program, a bug in the service that told you who was logged in, and the habit of trusting any login that came from a machine on your own list. None of this was secret. That was the point.

It was meant to spread quietly. A mistake in the part that checked whether a machine was already infected meant it kept reinfecting the same hosts, and by the small hours those hosts were running dozens of copies and could do nothing else. Around six thousand machines were affected, something like a tenth of everything connected. Sites pulled their own plugs to stop it coming in, and then could not read the email that explained what it was. Harold's lab spent two days with the network cable on the desk instead of in the wall.

Two things came out of it. The first was a team whose job was to coordinate the next time, which became the first CERT. The second was a question nobody had asked seriously before: why can any machine on the network talk to any port on mine?

The early answers were lists in routers, refusing packets by address and port before forwarding them. Then in 1994 a young Israeli company called Check Point shipped FireWall-1 and sold it on a phrase: stateful inspection. The box did not look at each packet alone. It remembered the conversation. Ruth bought one for the ISP a couple of years later and had never, she said, liked a product so much or trusted one so little.

The idea

A firewall is a guard at the door with a list. Packets arrive, the guard compares each one with the list, and the packet goes through or it does not. That is the whole job. Everything else is detail about what is on the list and how much the guard remembers.

The simplest kind is a packet filter. It looks at one packet at a time and only at the envelope: where it came from, where it is going, which protocol, which port. A rule might say allow TCP to port 25 on the mail server from anywhere or refuse everything to port 23. Packet filters are fast and dumb. Their weakness is replies. If a machine inside is allowed to open a connection out, the answers have to be allowed back in, and a filter that cannot tell an answer from a fresh attempt has to leave a gap for anything that looks like one. Attackers learned to make their packets look like answers.

A stateful firewall closes that gap by remembering. When it sees the first packet of a connection go out, the SYN from chapter 7, it writes down the pair of addresses and ports. When the reply comes back it checks the note and lets it through. A packet that matches no note and no rule is treated as a stranger.

The list can be written two ways round. A list of things to refuse lets everything else in; a list of things to allow refuses everything else. The second is called default deny, and after 1988 it became the rule for anything facing the outside. You do not list what is dangerous. You list what is needed, and the guard turns away the rest.

Some machines have to be reachable from outside, or there would be no point having a connection. The pattern that emerged was the DMZ, a demilitarised zone: a small network between two guards, holding only the things the outside is meant to see, such as the web server and the mail relay. The outside can reach the DMZ. The DMZ can reach a few named things inside. Nothing outside reaches inside directly.

When the guard turns a packet away there are two ways to do it. Reject sends something back: a TCP reset, or a small error note, so the sender learns at once that the door is shut and gives up. Drop sends nothing. The packet vanishes, the sender waits for its own timer to run out, tries again, waits again, and then reports a timeout. Drop is the default almost everywhere, because it tells an attacker nothing and costs the guard nothing. The price is paid by honest senders, who cannot tell a shut door from an empty building.

Remember it as: A firewall is a guard with a list; stateful means it remembers who went out so it can let the reply back in.

Put all of this together and you have the perimeter model: a hard shell around a soft centre. One boundary, well guarded. Inside it, machines trust each other, because the guard already checked. The model is older than the cloud, and the cloud borrowed its words and its habits. Every VPC has lists at its edges, and the guard still drops rather than rejects.

That is why Nadia's capture looked the way it did. A refusal would have come back in a millisecond as connection refused. Silence for sixty seconds is a packet dropped on purpose, by something with a list, and the list was not in her account.

⚠Where it breaks
  • Worm attack: a program copies itself to the next machine through an open service and a known hole, and that machine does the same. The sign is every machine slowing at once and the same strange process on all of them. Default deny at the boundary and patched services stop it getting in; guards between internal networks stop it spreading.
  • Open port exposure attack: a service listens on every address with no rule in front of it, and a scanner finds it within minutes. The sign is a log full of login attempts from addresses you have never heard of. Allow only what must be public, and put it in the DMZ.
  • Silent drop read as a slow server: a firewall drops a packet and says nothing, the client reports a timeout, and a team spends the evening tuning a server that never received anything. The tell is a connect timeout where a refusal would have been instant, and nothing at all in the server's logs. Check for a list at every hop before you touch the server.
  • Hard shell, soft centre: once inside the perimeter everything trusts everything, so one phished laptop can reach the database. The sign is no rules at all between internal networks. Put guards between internal networks too, not only at the door.

…but

On the walk to the station Nadia thought about the grey box the customers were seeing. 504 Gateway Time-out. Checkout's own log said connect timeout, and nobody at Kettle had written either sentence. Something between the phone and the pod was giving up first, and speaking for both of them.

The problem

At 08:00 on Saturday Nadia was at her kitchen table with the laptop, the notebook and the Kettle app open on her phone. The overnight numbers were worse: since the restart at 17:30, four checkouts in five were failing. Sam had posted a screenshot from a customer. A spinner, then the grey box.

She tried it herself and counted under her breath. The spinner turned for thirty seconds, almost exactly, and the box appeared. She tried from the laptop, against the same address the app used, and asked for the time.

$ curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} after %{time_total}s\n' -X POST https://kettle.example/api/checkout
504 after 30.04s

Thirty seconds. Then she opened the checkout logs for the same minute.

08:03:12 checkout-7d9f  POST /checkout  error="connect timeout"  peer=10.20.4.31:443  waited=60.0s

Sixty seconds. She rang Ruth, who answered on the second ring and sounded as if she had been up for hours.

"The customer gets a 504 at thirty seconds," Nadia said. "Checkout gives up at sixty. So when the customer sees the error, checkout is still waiting. It's still trying. For another half a minute."

"Who sends the 504?"

"Not checkout. It never got that far." She looked at the path in her notebook, the one Ruth had made her draw on Friday. Phone, CDN, load balancer, pod. "The load balancer. It's the thing that hands requests to the pods. It waits thirty seconds for a pod to answer, and then it answers for the pod."

"And what does the phone do when it gets a 504?"

Nadia looked at the app. The grey box had a button on it. The button said Try again.

◷Back then

In March 1989 a software engineer at CERN named Tim Berners-Lee wrote a document called Information Management: A Proposal and gave it to his manager. CERN had thousands of people, most of them passing through, and the things they knew lived in incompatible systems on incompatible machines. When someone left, what they knew left with them. His proposal was for a web of documents that pointed at one another across the network, so that any document anywhere could link to any other. His manager's note on the cover, since reproduced many times, called it vague but exciting.

By the end of 1990 he had built the three pieces it needed on a NeXT workstation: a way to name a document anywhere on the network, a short protocol for asking for it, and a format for writing pages with links in them. Those became the URL, HTTP and HTML. On 6 August 1991 he posted a summary of the project to a public discussion group and invited anyone to try it. That is the date people give for the web going public. It was, at that point, a handful of servers.

Ruth was on leased lines in 1989 and at the ISP by the time it mattered. "In 1994," she said, "every call from a business customer was about the web. Not email. The web. And the web had one problem for a shop: it forgot you between pages."

HTTP had been built for documents. Each request stood alone. The server answered and remembered nothing, which was the reason it could serve the world from a workstation. For a shop that meant a basket could not survive from one page to the next. In 1994 Lou Montulli, a young engineer at Netscape, fixed it with a small addition: the server could hand the browser a scrap of text, and the browser would send it back with every later request to the same site. He called it a cookie. It was the first time the web had a memory, and it was in the client, not the server.

The idea

Everything in this book so far has been envelopes. HTTP is the letter inside them. It is the thing the phone wrote and the thing checkout read, and it is short enough to read by eye.

A URL names what you want: a scheme such as https, a host such as kettle.example, an optional port (443 if the scheme is https and you say nothing), a path such as /api/checkout, and sometimes a query after a ?. The host part goes to DNS. The rest goes in the request.

An HTTP request is a few lines of text. The first line carries a method, the verb, and the path. GET asks for something and promises not to change anything. POST sends something that will change things, such as an order. PUT and DELETE do what they say. After the first line come headers, one per line, each a name and a value: Host says which site you mean, Content-Type says what the body is, Cookie carries the scrap of memory. Then a blank line, then the body, if there is one.

The response has the same shape the other way round. Its first line carries a status code, a three-digit number whose first digit tells you the kind of answer. 2xx is success, 200 the usual one. 3xx means look elsewhere. 4xx means the request was wrong: 404 for a path that is not there, 403 for not allowed. 5xx means the server side failed: 500 is a crash, 503 is overloaded, and 502 and 504 are special. They are not sent by the server you asked for. They are sent by something in between, on its behalf, to say that it could not get an answer: 502 for a bad one, 504 for none at all in the time allowed.

HTTP is stateless: each request stands alone, and the server keeps nothing between one and the next. That is what lets one address serve millions, and what lets any pod of forty-one answer any request. A cookie is how a site remembers you anyway. The server sends a Set-Cookie header with a value it will recognise, the browser stores it, and sends it back as a Cookie header on every later request to that site. The memory lives in the client. The server only has to recognise the token when it comes back.

Every hop a request passes through has a timeout: how long it will wait for the next hop before it stops waiting and tells the one behind it. The phone has one. The load balancer has one. Checkout has one for Paystream. Each was set by a different person on a different day, and nothing makes them agree. Whichever hop has the shortest clock speaks first, and it speaks for everything behind it.

Hop Waits for Gives up after
Phone app load balancer ?
Load balancer checkout pod 30 s
Checkout pod Paystream 60 s

Remember it as: HTTP is a letter and a reply, each standing alone; cookies are the memory; every hop on the way has its own clock.

The question mark in that table was in Nadia's notebook, and she did not like it. At Kettle the load balancer's thirty seconds ran out first, so the customer saw a 504 while checkout was still waiting for a SYN-ACK that would never come. For the next thirty seconds that pod was busy doing nothing, and the customer had a button that said Try again.

⚠Where it breaks
  • Cookie theft attack: the cookie is the session, so whoever holds it is you. It is taken from a plain-text connection or by a script smuggled into the page. The sign is activity in an account from a device its owner has never used; TLS, the Secure and HttpOnly flags and short-lived sessions stop it.
  • Mismatched timeouts across hops: the hop in front gives up before the hop behind, so the customer sees an error while the work continues, and a retry starts a second copy of it. The sign is 504s at the edge with no matching error, or a later one, in the application. Make every timeout shorter than the one in front of it, and write them all on one page.
  • Retrying a POST: a request that changes something is sent again after a timeout, and the first one had worked. The sign is a customer charged twice for one bag of beans. Give each order a key the server can recognise, so the second copy is answered, not repeated.
  • Status codes that lie: a 200 with an error in the body, or a 500 for a request the client got wrong. The sign is a dashboard full of green while the support inbox fills. Use the codes as they were meant, and alert on 5xx.

…but

Sam rang at twenty-five past eight. He had been reading the cloud provider's documentation in bed, which was never a good sign, and he had an idea. The endpoint had a hostname of its own, a long one. What if checkout called that, and left api.paystream.example out of it?

The problem

Sam's idea, at 08:30, went like this. The endpoint in the platform account had a hostname of its own, generated by the cloud: vpce-0f3a9c1d7b2e.pay.endpoints.cloud.example. It pointed at the same three private addresses. Checkout's configuration held the Paystream address as a URL. Change the URL to the endpoint's own name, and whatever DNS was doing to api.paystream.example would stop mattering. "It's a config change in our account," he said. "We can ship that. If it's DNS, that's the fix."

Nadia did not think it was DNS any more, but she had learned to test the idea rather than argue with it. The endpoint name would not resolve from her kitchen, so she looked instead at what Paystream would present when a connection arrived. From the laptop, against the public address, she asked for the certificate and read the names on it.

$ openssl s_client -connect api.paystream.example:443 </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -ext subjectAltName
X509v3 Subject Alternative Name:
    DNS:api.paystream.example, DNS:*.paystream.example

Two names, both Paystream's. Nothing under cloud.example. A client told to call vpce-0f3a9c1d7b2e.pay.endpoints.cloud.example would connect, be handed this certificate, look for its own hostname on the list, and hang up.

"Then skip the name," said Sam. "Hard-code 10.20.4.31. It's not going to move."

She tried the equivalent from the kitchen, against Paystream's public address.

$ curl https://203.0.113.10/v1/ping
curl: (60) SSL: no alternative certificate subject name matches target host name '203.0.113.10'

"Same thing," she said. "The client checks the name it was asked for against the certificate. An address isn't on it either."

"There's a flag to turn that check off."

Ruth, who had been on the call the whole time and silent, spoke for the first time. "There is. And then anyone standing between you and Paystream can be Paystream, and you'll pay them."

◷Back then

In 1995 Ruth's ISP had one customer who sold things, a stationery firm with a catalogue, and what they wanted was the padlock. Netscape had put it there. Its browser was the one everyone used, and that year the company shipped a protocol called SSL, the Secure Sockets Layer, so that a card number typed into a page would travel scrambled. The work was led by Taher Elgamal, and its first public version was numbered 2.0, because the first had been found wanting before it left the building. Within a year there was a 3.0, with the holes of 2.0 patched. The padlock in the corner of the window was the whole product. Nobody outside a few universities could have said what it did.

The protocol belonged to one company, and the other browsers did not want to carry a rival's name. The standards body took it over, and in January 1999 published it as TLS 1.0, Transport Layer Security. The name change was the price of agreement. The protocol underneath was SSL 3.0 with the edges filed down. "Everyone kept calling it SSL anyway," Ruth said. "They still do."

For the next fifteen years the padlock stayed where the money was. A certificate cost real money and a form, renewed by hand, and most of the web stayed plain because nobody could be bothered. That changed in 2015, when a project called Let's Encrypt issued its first certificate: free, automatic, renewed by a script. Within a few years most pages on the web were encrypted, and the browsers started to warn about the ones that were not.

The protocol itself kept being repaired. In August 2018 TLS 1.3 was published. It threw out every old way of agreeing a key that had turned out to be weak, and it cut the handshake to one round trip. Ruth had moved Kettle's last on-premises box to the cloud by then. The certificates renewed themselves. She did not miss the forms.

The idea

TLS is a sealed, tamper-evident envelope with a verified return address. It wraps a connection, usually a TCP one, and gives the two ends three things. Privacy: nobody in between can read what is inside. Integrity: nobody in between can change it without the change being noticed. Identity: the client knows which server it is talking to. HTTPS is HTTP inside that envelope, on port 443 instead of 80. Every other protocol this book meets later can go inside the same envelope.

The hard part is the third thing. Scrambling bytes is well understood. Knowing that the machine you are scrambling them for is Paystream, and not something between you and Paystream, needs a piece of paper.

A certificate is that paper: a statement, signed by a certificate authority that your client already trusts, that the holder of a particular key is entitled to a list of names. The list is what matters here. It is a list of DNS names, such as api.paystream.example, and it can carry a wildcard such as *.paystream.example. It very rarely carries an IP address. When a client connects, the server presents the certificate and proves it holds the key. The client checks three things: that the signature leads back to an authority it trusts, that the dates are current, and that the name it was asked to call is on the list. Fail any of the three and the client hangs up before a byte of HTTP is sent.

The first message carries the name the client wants, in the clear, before anything is sealed. That is SNI, Server Name Indication, and it exists because one address often serves many names. Without it the server would have to guess which certificate to show before the client had said which site it wanted. With it, the client says the name, the server picks the matching paper, and the check can succeed.

That is why the name is the thing. The client decides what name it is calling, from the URL it was given. The certificate lists names. If the two do not meet, there is no connection, however correct the address underneath. Tell a client to call 10.20.4.31 and it will look for 10.20.4.31 on the list.

The check is not fussiness. Anyone who can sit between a client and a server, at a café router, at an ISP, or at a private address inside a VPC, can accept the client's connection and open their own to the real server, reading and changing everything that passes. That is a man-in-the-middle, and the certificate check is the only thing that stops it. The attacker can present a certificate, but not one with the right name signed by an authority the client trusts. Turn the check off and the envelope is still sealed. It is sealed to whoever answered.

The handshake costs a round trip in TLS 1.3, two in older versions, on top of the one TCP needs. For a request a second that is nothing. For a new connection on every request it adds up, which is why clients keep connections open and why a later chapter cares about that.

Remember it as: TLS seals the envelope and checks the return address: the name you asked for must be on the certificate, or you hang up.

How the keys are agreed, what the signatures are made of and how an authority earns trust are the business of Cybersecurity: The Keep. For this book the point is the name. Sam's shortcut failed because the check was doing its job: Paystream's certificate names Paystream, and the endpoint's hostname belongs to the cloud. The connection would be sealed and would go nowhere.

⚠Where it breaks
  • Man-in-the-middle attack: someone between the two ends accepts the client's connection, opens their own to the server, and relays both ways while reading everything. The sign is a certificate warning, or none at all if verification was switched off. Verify the chain and the name, and never ship a client with the check disabled.
  • Certificate name mismatch: a client is told to call a server by a name, or an address, that the certificate does not list. The sign is an error that quotes the hostname and happens before any HTTP is sent. Call the server by a name on its certificate, or get a certificate that includes the name you use.
  • Expired certificate: the dates on the paper run out, and every client hangs up at once. The sign is an outage at midnight on a day nobody changed anything. Renew automatically and alert weeks ahead.
  • Verification switched off "for now": a flag set to make a test pass, then shipped. The sign is verify=false or its cousins in a config file with no comment, and a padlock that is still drawn but means nothing. Treat the flag as a bug and remove it.

…but

At 09:10 Sam's approval came through: a read-only role in the platform account, at last. Nadia clicked the console link, signed in, and got one line in return. Sign-in from this network is not permitted.

The problem

Sign-in from this network is not permitted. Nadia read it three times. The role was real. Sam had sent her the confirmation. The platform account's console had looked at where her request came from, which at 09:30 on a Saturday was a kitchen in a flat with a broadband router, and shut the door.

"It's allowed from the office," Sam said. "Jonas locked it down after the audit. The console only takes sign-ins from the office address."

"I can be in the office in forty minutes."

"Or," said Ruth, "you can bring the office to you. There's a VPN. It runs on one of my beige boxes. It's on the handover list, page four."

Nadia had used the VPN once, in her first week, to reach a printer. She opened the client, signed in with her usual account and a code from her phone, and watched the small icon turn from grey to green. Then she asked a public website what address it saw her coming from, before and after.

$ curl -s https://myaddr.example/      # home broadband
81.2.69.144
$ curl -s https://myaddr.example/      # with the VPN up
198.51.100.20

The second address was Kettle's. Her packets were leaving the flat sealed, arriving at the office, being unwrapped there and going out again through the office's front door, so that the console saw them coming from the building. The video call with Sam stuttered and froze, because the video was now going to the office and back as well.

She reloaded the console. It let her in. For the first time since Friday afternoon she could see the platform account: the shared subnets in 10.20.0.0/16, the endpoints, and in the list of endpoints, one created at 15:58 the day before, named paystream-private.

◷Back then

The first network Ruth ever ordered came from the telephone company, and it came slowly. It was the mid-eighties. A firm with two offices that wanted to connect them did not use the internet, because the internet was for universities. It rented a leased line: a circuit, in the chapter 2 sense, held open permanently between two buildings and billed by the month and the mile. You filled in a form, waited some weeks for an engineer, and then had a wire that was yours and nobody else's. Large companies built whole private networks this way, office to office, and the bill for them was a line item the board could see.

By 1995 Ruth was at the ISP, and the economics had turned over. Her customers already had a line to the internet; a second line to their other office cost many times more and did far less. What they wanted was to use the public network as if it were private. The piece that made this respectable arrived in August 1995, when the standards body published the first IPsec documents, written by Randall Atkinson at the US Naval Research Laboratory. IPsec put security into the IP layer itself. A packet could be sealed, given a check that would show tampering, and wrapped in a new outer packet addressed to a gateway at the far end. The gateway unwrapped it and put the original on the private network as if it had never left.

"We sold it as a leased line for a tenth of the price," Ruth said. "Which was true, and the first customer rang me on the Monday to say the office in Swindon could see the file server in Reading and could we take the leased line out. We could. The telephone company took another six weeks."

The remote kind came later, in the same shape: one laptop, one gateway, a tunnel on demand. First with IPsec clients that fought with every hotel firewall, then with tunnels that ran inside TLS on port 443, because port 443 was the one door nobody shut.

The idea

A VPN, a virtual private network, is a diplomatic pouch. Your packets travel through the public post, sealed, addressed to an embassy, and when the pouch is opened on the other side the letters inside are delivered as if they had been posted there. The public network carries them. It cannot read them, and it does not know where they are really going.

The mechanism is the envelopes-inside-envelopes trick from chapter 5, with a seal. The laptop builds a packet for a private address, say the office file server. Instead of sending it, a VPN client encrypts the whole packet and puts it inside a new one addressed to the VPN gateway, a machine with a public address at the edge of the private network. The outer packet crosses the home router, the ISP and the internet like any other. The gateway strips the outer packet, checks the seal, and forwards the inner one onto the private network. Replies come back the same way in reverse.

IPsec does the sealing at the IP layer, packet by packet, which suits gateways. The other common kind, a TLS VPN, carries the same inner packets inside a TLS connection on port 443, which suits laptops behind hotel firewalls. The shape is the same. What differs is which layer does the wrapping.

There are two ways to use a tunnel. Site-to-site joins two networks: a gateway at each end, always on, and nobody in either office knows it is there. This is what replaced the leased line, and it is what joins an office to a cloud network in a later chapter. Remote access joins one machine to a network on demand: the laptop at the kitchen table becomes, for as long as the icon is green, a machine in the office.

How much becomes the office is a choice. With split tunnelling only traffic for the private ranges goes through the tunnel, and everything else, the video call and the music, goes straight out of the home router as before. With a full tunnel everything goes through the office, which is why Nadia's call froze. Full tunnels are safer in one way, since the office sees and can filter everything, and worse in another, since the office link now carries every employee's video.

Remember it as: A VPN is a diplomatic pouch: your packets travel sealed through the public post and come out inside the office.

Now put this next to chapter 15. The firewall drew a line around the building and trusted what was inside. The VPN moves that line. A laptop in a kitchen, on a home network the company has never seen, is inside the perimeter, with the perimeter's trust, and the guard at the door sees a colleague. That is the VPN's whole value and its whole risk. Everything the laptop has picked up comes in with it, and anyone holding its credentials comes in from anywhere. The ciphers and the seals belong to Cybersecurity: The Keep. The network lesson is shorter: a rule that trusts an address lets in whoever can arrange to have that address.

That is what let Nadia in: the console trusted the office's address, the VPN gave her the office's address, and the lock had checked where she came from, not who she was.

⚠Where it breaks
  • Stolen VPN credentials attack: a password from a leaked list, no second factor, and the attacker is inside the perimeter from a city they have never visited. The sign is one account signing in from two countries in an hour. A second factor and a certificate on the device stop it, and so does refusing to treat "inside" as "trusted".
  • Unpatched VPN gateway attack: the gateway is a public open port by design, and holes in gateway software are a favourite way in. The sign is a vendor advisory you have not applied. Patch it first, and limit what the tunnel can reach once through.
  • Full tunnel surprises: everything goes through the office, so video stutters, the office line fills up, and sites the office blocks are blocked at home too. The sign is a complaint that "the VPN is slow" when the office line is the thing that is slow. Split the tunnel, with care about what stays outside.
  • Split tunnel leaks: the laptop is on two networks at once, and a private name is looked up through the home resolver or a private range is routed out of the home router. The sign is a VPN that connects but cannot find anything by name. Send the private ranges and their DNS through the tunnel, and nothing else.
  • Overlapping ranges: the home network and the office both use 192.168.1.0/24, and the laptop cannot tell which side a packet is for. The sign is a tunnel that comes up and a file server that never answers. Give the office a private range nobody's home router would choose.

…but

The endpoint named paystream-private had a status column. Nadia clicked through. Three network interfaces, one per zone, 10.20.4.31 among them, and next to each a green tick and the word Healthy. Something had checked those interfaces in the last minute and found them well. Checkout had been trying for seventeen hours and had never once got an answer.
