The problem

The VPN had taken three attempts and a code from her phone, and now the platform account's console was open on the kitchen table. Nadia had never been inside it. It looked like Kettle's own account, the same grey menus in the same places, but the names in it were Jonas's names, and there were more of them than she expected.

She searched for "paystream". One object, created on Friday at 15:58, state available. Three network interfaces, one in each of the endpoint subnets, and there, in a neat row, were the addresses she had been chasing since Friday evening.

vpce-0f3a9c1d7b2e   paystream-private   available   created Fri 15:58
  10.20.4.31   10.20.5.31   10.20.6.31
  provider health: healthy (3 of 3)

"Healthy," she said into the phone. Ruth had rung at ten from her kitchen in Reading and said she would stay on the line while she did the crossword. "Three of three. Everything on this page says it's fine."

"Who sends the health checks?"

Nadia read the line again. It belonged to the provider's side: Paystream's own load balancer, checking Paystream's own servers behind the endpoint. "Paystream does. To itself."

"From where?"

"From inside Paystream."

"And your balancer. The one in front of checkout. What does it check?"

She opened Kettle's account, the one she knew. Forty-one targets, forty-one healthy. The check was a GET to /healthz every ten seconds, and /healthz returned 200 whenever the process was running. It did not call Paystream. It did not call anything.

"So," said Ruth. "Two sets of green lights, and not one of them has ever sent a packet from a pod to that endpoint. You've been reading a thermometer that isn't in the patient."

Nadia wrote it down and underlined it: health checks test the checker's path, not the customer's.

◷Back then

Ruth's first load balancer arrived in a cardboard box in 1996, and she had not asked for it.

The ISP in Reading hosted websites for anyone who would pay, and one of them was a weekly music paper that had put its singles chart online. On Sunday evenings, when the chart was read out on the radio, the paper's one server fell over. Not slowed: fell over, with a queue of half-opened connections it never finished. Ruth's colleague Dev, who did the hosting, bought a second machine and copied the site onto it. Then they had a problem neither of them had met before. Two machines, one name. Which one should the name point at?

The only tool they had was DNS. Dev put both addresses in the record and the name server handed them out in turn, first one, then the other, round and round. It was called round-robin DNS and it worked for about a fortnight. Then the second machine's disk died on a bank holiday Monday, and for the whole of that day half the readers were sent to a dead server, because DNS has no idea whether the thing it names is alive. The other half were fine. Ruth remembered the phone calls: it works for me, it doesn't work for me, both true, and nobody able to say why.

The box that came later that year held one address on the front and two cables on the back. It answered the name itself. For every new connection it chose a server, and every few seconds it asked each server a small question and crossed off the ones that did not answer. Dev plugged it in on a Friday and nobody at the music paper ever noticed, which Ruth said was the highest compliment the thing could be paid.

"That was the day I stopped thinking of a name as a machine," she told Nadia. "A name is a desk. Who sits at it is somebody else's problem."

The idea

A load balancer is a machine, or a managed service, that owns one address and stands in front of many servers. Clients connect to the one address. The balancer passes each connection, or each request, to one of the servers behind it and sends the answer back. It is the reception desk: one address on the door, visitors sent to any free clerk, and nobody outside needing to know how many clerks there are today.

The cheapest way to have one name and many servers is round-robin DNS: give the name several A records and let the name server hand them out in rotation. It costs nothing and it half works. DNS does not know which servers are alive, so a dead one stays in the rotation until a person removes it, and resolvers cache whichever answer they got for the record's TTL, so clients are pinned to one server for minutes at a time. It is still used to spread traffic across balancers in different regions; behind the name, a real balancer does the work.

There are two kinds, named after the layers from chapter 5. An L4 load balancer works at the transport layer: it sees addresses and ports, picks a server for each new TCP connection and forwards the packets, never reading what is inside. It is fast and it understands nothing. An L7 load balancer works at the application layer: it reads the HTTP request and can send /api/pay to one set of servers and /images to another, add a header, or reject a bad request before any server sees it. To do that it has to be a reverse proxy: a server that accepts the client's connection, makes its own separate connection to a backend, and copies the request across. Two connections, two handshakes, and the backend sees the proxy's address, not the client's, unless the proxy writes the client's address into a header. Kettle's public balancer is this kind.

L4 L7
Sees addresses, ports the HTTP request
Chooses per connection request
Can route by path no yes
Connection to backend the client's own its own

A balancer only knows what it asks. A health check is a small request it sends to every server every few seconds; a server that fails a few in a row is taken out of rotation until it passes again. The check is a question, and the question is chosen by whoever set the balancer up. "Is the process listening?" is the usual one. It is not "can this server do the thing customers need?", and the gap between those two questions is where Saturday morning's green lights came from.

Three more things ride on the balancer. A sticky session sends the same client back to the same server each time, by a cookie or by source address, for applications that keep state in memory. TLS termination is the balancer holding the certificate and ending the encrypted connection itself, so the certificate must carry the public name, as chapter 17 found, and the hop inside can be plain HTTP or a second TLS connection. And keep-alive is the agreement to keep a TCP connection open after a request so the next one can skip the handshake; a connection pool is a client holding several such open connections ready for reuse. Pools sit between the balancer and the pods, and between each pod and Paystream. They make everything faster, and they remember the world as it was when they were opened.

Remember it as: One address on the door, any free clerk behind it, and a reception desk that only knows what it asks.

At Kettle the balancer asks /healthz, and /healthz says yes while every payment behind it times out. Paystream's balancer asks its own servers, from its own side of the endpoint. Nobody is asking the question that matters, which is whether a pod can reach the address it has been given.

⚠Where it breaks
  • Health check that tests the wrong path: the check asks "are you listening?" while customers need "can you pay?", so servers that are dead in practice stay in rotation. The sign is a fleet that is all green while the error rate climbs. Make the check exercise the real dependency, or add a deeper check that drains the server when it fails, and be honest about what the balancer's check proves.
  • Round-robin DNS with a dead server: DNS keeps handing out the address of a machine that has gone. The sign is "it works for me" from half the callers. Put a balancer with health checks behind the name, and keep the TTL short.
  • Sticky sessions pinning the load: one server fills with the clients stuck to it while the others sit idle, and when it dies every stuck client loses their session. The sign is one hot server in a cold fleet. Keep session state out of the server, and let the balancer spread freely.
  • Stale pooled connection: the balancer closes an idle connection at 30 s and the client reuses it from its pool a moment later, so the first request fails with a reset. The sign is a sprinkle of errors on the first request after a quiet spell. Set the client's idle timeout shorter than the server's, and check a pooled connection before trusting it.

…but

At 10:25 Sam forwarded a message from Marketing. They had checked from four phones and a laptop, and the site was up, and could engineering please stop saying it was down.

The problem

Nadia loaded the storefront on her phone with the Wi-Fi off, the way Marketing would have. It was fast. The home page, the Ethiopian, the roaster in Leeds, the basket: all of it came up before she had finished lowering her thumb. She could see why they were cross.

Then she asked the site to tell her where the page had come from.

$ curl -sI https://www.kettle.example/ | grep -iE 'cache|age'
cache-control: public, max-age=3600
age: 2210
x-cache: HIT

Age 2210. The page in her hand had been made thirty-seven minutes ago and was being handed out again from a copy. The server that built it, Kettle's storefront pods behind Kettle's load balancer, had not been asked. She tried the checkout page.

$ curl -sI https://www.kettle.example/checkout | grep -iE 'cache|age'
cache-control: no-store
x-cache: MISS

No copy, by instruction. Every request for anything to do with paying went through to the origin, and from the origin to a pod, and from the pod to an address that did not answer.

"Marketing checked the forms," said Ruth, when Nadia explained it. "The branch office has plenty of forms. It doesn't have a cashier."

"So the site is up."

"The shop window is up. Tell Sam that, in those words. It'll save him a conversation with the CEO." A pause, and the scratch of a pencil. "And write down what 'up' meant to the person who said it. That's a fact about the incident, not a complaint about Marketing."

Nadia typed the shop window is up, the till is not into the channel, and three people reacted with a coffee cup.

◷Back then

By 1998 Ruth had watched the same thing happen a dozen times. A customer's site would be mentioned on the radio or in a newspaper, and within a minute the single line into that customer's single server would be full. The server was fine. The line was full. Everyone arrived at once, from everywhere, at one door, and the door was in Reading.

The problem had a name at MIT, where Tim Berners-Lee had been asking the mathematicians down the corridor whether anything could be done about "hot spots": the one server, the one pipe, the whole world arriving at the same moment. Tom Leighton, a professor of applied mathematics, took the question seriously, and so did his graduate student Danny Lewin. Their answer was not a faster server. It was to stop having one place at all. Put copies of the popular content on many machines in many cities, close to the people asking, and work out a way of deciding which copy lived where so that adding or losing a machine moved only a little of the content and not all of it. The mathematics for that last part was theirs, and in 1998 they founded a company on it and called it Akamai. The service went live the next year, and the early customers were the ones with the worst hot spots: a film trailer everyone wanted on the same afternoon, a sports tournament, news on a bad day.

Ruth remembered the first time she traced a request for a well-known site and watched it stop two hops away, at a machine inside somebody else's network, which handed back the page as if it owned it.

"It felt like cheating," she said. "It still does, a bit. But the line into Reading stopped filling up, and that was the point."

The idea

A cache is a copy kept close so the next request does not have to go all the way to the source. Your browser has one. So does the resolver from chapter 11; a cached DNS answer is the same idea with a TTL on it. The web's largest caches belong to a CDN, a content delivery network: many servers in many cities that hold copies of a site's pages, images and scripts and answer for the site in its own name. Each of those places is an edge location, a building with servers near a large population and good connections to the local networks, and the server you own, the one behind the load balancer from chapter 19, is the origin. The branch office holds copies of the popular forms; the head office prints them.

A request reaches the nearest edge first. If the edge has a fresh copy, it answers at once, and the origin never hears about it. If not, the edge fetches from the origin, keeps a copy if it is allowed to, and answers. What "allowed" means comes from the origin's own headers: cache-control: public, max-age=3600 says anyone may keep this for an hour; no-store says nobody may keep it at all. A checkout page, a basket, anything that differs per person or changes the world when you ask for it, is no-store, and for it the edge is only a corridor.

How does a phone in Leeds find the Manchester edge? Two ways. The CDN's DNS can look at where the question came from and answer with the address of a nearby edge, which is round-robin DNS with a map. Or the CDN uses anycast: the same address is announced from every edge location at once, through the BGP of chapter 13, and the ordinary routing of the internet carries each packet to whichever announcement is nearest. One address, two hundred buildings, and your packet goes to the closest one without anyone choosing. It also means a flood aimed at that address is split across all two hundred, which is a point the next chapter needs.

What the edge keeps is filed under a cache key: usually the full URL, sometimes with a header or two, such as the language. Two requests with the same key get the same copy, which is why a page that differs by user must say so or be no-store. A copy lives until its age passes its max-age, or until the origin tells the edge to forget it early, which is cache invalidation, also called a purge. Invalidation is the part everyone gets wrong, because it is the only part that needs the origin to remember every place it has left a copy. The edge also stands between the internet and the origin as a security layer, where a WAF, a web application firewall, inspects each request for attacks on the application itself; that work belongs to Cybersecurity: The Keep.

Remember it as: The branch office has copies of the popular forms, so "the site is up" only means the forms are in stock.

Kettle's storefront is a shelf of forms with an hour on them, and the edge has been handing them out since Friday without needing anyone in the building. Checkout is no-store. It walks past the shelf, through the origin, into a pod, and stops.

⚠Where it breaks
  • Stale cache after deploy: you ship a fix and the edge keeps serving the old page until its max-age runs out, or for ever if the key never changes. The sign is "fixed on my machine, broken for customers" for the length of one max-age. Put a version in the filename of anything long-lived, keep pages short-lived, and purge on deploy.
  • Personal page cached as public: a page that includes a name or a basket gets a public cache header and the next visitor sees someone else's order. The sign is a customer reporting another customer's details. Mark anything per-user private or no-store, and never let the cache key ignore what makes a page personal.
  • Origin reached directly attack: an attacker finds the origin's own address and sends traffic past the edge, past the WAF and past the cache. The sign is requests at the origin that never passed through an edge. Allow the origin to answer only the CDN's addresses, and keep its address out of DNS.
  • Monitoring the shelf: the uptime check fetches the home page, the edge answers from cache, and the check stays green through an outage. The sign is this morning. Make at least one check do something that cannot be cached.

…but

At 10:50 the load balancer's own graph moved. Requests to checkout were climbing, double what a Saturday morning should carry and still rising, and Sam asked the question the whole channel had been thinking. "Are we being attacked as well?"

Chapter 21 · Act IVThe Flood#

The problem

Nadia had seen the shape before, on a slide at a conference: a flat line and then a cliff going the wrong way. Requests to /api/pay were running at six times a normal Saturday and the balancer's queue was growing. If she had been told nothing else she would have said the same as Sam.

She looked at where it was coming from. Not a thousand strangers. One user agent, Kettle's own mobile app, and a short list of customers. She picked one order number and searched the checkout logs for it.

10:58:31 pay order=K-88213 req=a71 try=1 paystream: connect timeout 60 s
10:59:31 pay order=K-88213 req=a71 try=2 paystream: connect timeout 60 s
11:00:31 pay order=K-88213 req=a71 try=3 paystream: connect timeout 60 s
11:01:33 pay order=K-88213 req=c09 try=1 paystream: connect timeout 60 s

One order. Checkout had tried Paystream three times, a minute apart, with nothing between the tries except the wait for the timeout. Then a new request number: the app, having heard nothing, had sent the whole order again. She scrolled. Three app requests, three tries each. Nine attempts for one tap, each one holding a checkout worker for a minute, and the customer, who had seen only a spinner and a grey box, pressing the button again.

"What's between the tries?" asked Ruth.

"Nothing. Try, wait sixty seconds, try."

"And the app?"

"The same. Three times, no wait."

"Then nobody is attacking you," said Ruth. "You're doing it to yourselves. Multiply it out."

Nadia did. A third of customers failing on Friday evening, each becoming nine, had been a nuisance. By Saturday morning, with four in five failing and every failure taking a full minute, the nine had become the load.

She wrote retry storm in the notebook with a question mark, and then crossed the question mark out.

◷Back then

In February 2000 Ruth was running the network for the ISP in Reading, and on a Monday evening she watched the news report that Yahoo!, then the busiest site in the world, had been unreachable for most of the American morning. Over the following days it was eBay, then CNN, then Amazon. Nothing had been broken into. The sites had been buried. Someone had taken over computers at universities, pointed them all at one target and told them to send as much as they could, so the pipes into the biggest sites on the internet filled with rubbish and the real customers could not get through the door.

The someone turned out to be a fifteen-year-old in Montreal who called himself Mafiaboy, and the lesson Ruth took from him was that the server was not the target. The road was. A perfect server at the end of a full road is a server nobody can reach.

Sixteen years later, on 21 October 2016, she was sitting in a meeting when half the room's tools stopped working. Twitter, GitHub, Spotify, Reddit, a dozen others: unreachable across much of the east coast of America, in waves through the day. None of them had been attacked. Their DNS provider, a company called Dyn, had been, and when directory enquiries goes down the shops might as well have. The attacker this time was a program called Mirai, and the computers it had taken over were not at universities. They were cameras, video recorders and home routers, hundreds of thousands of them, still set to the password printed on the box.

"Harold used to say the dumb network can't tell a customer from a flood," Ruth said. "He was right then and he was right in 2016. It isn't the network's job. It's yours."

The idea

A denial of service, DoS, is an attack that makes something unavailable not by breaking in but by using it up: the bandwidth of a line, the table of half-open connections, the memory of a server, the patience of a queue. A DDoS is the distributed kind, from many machines at once, so that no single address can be blocked and the total is larger than any one line could carry. In the postal picture it is a million junk letters to one address. The letterbox is full, the postman cannot get the real post in, and the person inside has done nothing wrong.

There are three places to hit: the pipe, with more bytes than the line can carry; the protocol, with the first packet of chapter 7's handshake sent over and over and never the third, until the server's table of half-open connections is full; and the application, with requests that are cheap to make and expensive to answer.

The pipe is the easiest to fill, because of two tricks. Reflection is sending a request to an innocent third party with the source address forged to be the victim's; the reply goes to the victim. UDP makes this possible, because a postcard needs no handshake and so carries no proof of who sent it. Amplification is choosing a third party whose answers are much bigger than its questions, so that a small stream of forged questions becomes a large stream of unwanted answers. A DNS query of sixty bytes can return an answer of three thousand; other services have done worse.

The many machines usually belong to someone else. A botnet is a collection of computers an attacker has taken over and can command together, and since Mirai the computers need not be computers; anything with a network port and a default password will do.

The defences are layered. Rate limiting is the application refusing to do more than so many requests per second for one client, one token or one address, and answering the rest with a quick "later" that costs almost nothing. Scrubbing is diverting all traffic for a site through a centre that drops the rubbish and forwards the rest, usually by announcing the site's prefix from the scrubbing centre for the length of the attack. And anycast absorption is the CDN trick from the last chapter: an address announced from two hundred edges spreads any flood across two hundred buildings, and no single line fills.

None of that would have helped Kettle on Saturday morning, because the flood was coming from inside. A retry is a client trying again after a failure. A retry storm is what happens when every layer does it, each on its own, and none of them waits. The app retries three times. Checkout retries three times. Three times three is nine attempts for one tap, and the service they are all aimed at is the one that is already failing, which now fails more slowly, which makes every attempt take longer, which fills more workers, which fails more customers, who press the button again.

The cure is as old as chapter 7, where Van Jacobson's fix for a congested network was for every sender to wait longer after each failure. Backoff means waiting, and waiting longer each time, before a retry; jitter means adding a random amount so that a thousand clients that failed together do not retry together. Beyond that: retry at one layer, not every layer; give the whole operation a budget of attempts; and stop sending for a while when almost everything is failing. Those are not network settings. They are lines in the app and in checkout.

Remember it as: A flood doesn't care who sent it: a million junk letters or your own retries, the letterbox fills the same way.

Saturday's spike was never an attack. It was Friday's failure, multiplied by nine, arriving at the one address that could not answer it.

⚠Where it breaks
  • Reflection and amplification attack: an attacker forges the victim's address on small UDP questions to open servers, which send their large answers to the victim. The sign is inbound traffic from DNS or time servers the victim never asked. Networks should drop packets whose source address could not have come from them, and servers should not answer the whole internet.
  • Botnet attack: thousands of taken-over devices send ordinary-looking traffic at once, so there is no single address to block. The sign is a crowd of real-looking clients that all arrived in the same minute. Absorb it at anycast edges, scrub it, and rate-limit whatever gets through.
  • Retry storm: every layer retries, nobody waits, and a failing service receives several times its normal load from its own clients. The sign is traffic that rises as success falls, from your own user agents. Back off with jitter, retry in one place, and stop retrying when nearly everything fails.
  • Rate limit on the wrong key: a limit per source address, behind the carrier-grade NAT from chapter 14, throttles a whole mobile network's worth of customers because they share one address. The sign is one region's customers all locked out together. Limit by account or token, and allow bursts.

…but

The nine explained the flood. It did not explain the one number nobody had touched since Friday: at 16:02 a third of checkouts had failed and two thirds had gone through, on pods that were all running the same code and all asking the same name. Nadia went to find out which pods the successful ones had used.

The problem

By noon Nadia had a table she had not known she could make. The logs recorded which pod had served each checkout, and when each pod had started, and between 16:02 and 17:30 on Friday the pods fell into two groups so cleanly that she checked it twice.

pod            started       16:02 to 17:30     after 17:30
checkout-7f2   Thu 09:14     412 ok of 418      gone
checkout-9c1   Fri 16:11     3 ok of 301        gone
checkout-b40   Fri 17:31     -                  70 ok of 360

Pods running since Thursday kept paying people. Pods that started after four o'clock on Friday did not. At 17:30 somebody had restarted the lot, and every pod had become a pod that started after four o'clock. The seventy that still went through after that were paid with gift credit and had never called Paystream.

"What does the payment client do with its connections?" asked Ruth.

Nadia found the library's documentation. It kept a pool. On first use it looked the name up, opened a handful of connections to the answer, and reused them for every call afterwards, for as long as they stayed busy and the far end kept them open. There was a setting for how long to keep them, and Kettle had never changed it.

"So a pod from Thursday," she said slowly, "looked up api.paystream.example on Thursday. Got the public address. Opened its connections and kept them. When the answer changed on Friday, nobody told the connections, because a connection isn't to a name. It's to an address. The old pods never asked again."

"Until?"

"Until a connection in the pool died and it opened a new one. Then it asked, got 10.20.4.31, and that connection never came back. That's why it got worse through the evening." She looked at the third row. "And at 17:30 we closed every connection that was still working. To clear it."

"The restart didn't break anything," said Ruth. "It stopped the thing that was hiding the break."

Nadia drew a box round the table and wrote across the top: a third failed because a third of the connections were new.

◷Back then

The web Ruth hosted in 1997 was made of small pictures, and every one of them was a phone call. A page with thirty little GIFs meant thirty TCP handshakes, one after another, on a modem where each handshake took the better part of a second. HTTP/1.0 opened a connection, asked for one thing, and hung up. In January 1997 the standard for HTTP/1.1 was published, with Roy Fielding among its authors, and it changed two things Ruth cared about. The connection stayed open by default, so the thirty pictures could share one call. And every request now carried the name of the site it wanted, in a Host header, which meant she could put forty customers' sites on one address instead of forty addresses, and she had been running out of addresses.

Persistent connections had a limit, though. On one connection the answers had to come back in the order the questions were asked, so one slow picture held up the twenty-nine behind it. Browsers answered by opening six connections at a time, which was six handshakes and six queues on every server.

In November 2009 two engineers at Google, Mike Belshe and Roberto Peon, announced SPDY, an experiment in doing better: one connection, many requests in flight at once, answers in whatever order they were ready, headers compressed. It worked well enough that the standards people took it in nearly whole, and in May 2015 it became HTTP/2. Then Google went after the handshake itself. TCP and TLS together cost two or three round trips before the first byte of a request; QUIC put the transport on top of UDP, built the encryption in, and did the whole thing in one. The IETF published it as RFC 9000 in May 2021, and HTTP/3, which is HTTP over QUIC, followed in June 2022.

"Every one of those was about shaking hands less," Ruth said. "Which means holding on longer. A connection that's held on to for a day has opinions about the world that are a day old."

The idea

Chapter 19 introduced keep-alive as an agreement to leave a TCP connection open after a request. HTTP/1.1 made that the default, and it is still the HTTP most servers speak to each other. It has one rule that costs: on a single connection, responses come back in the order the requests were sent. If the first response is slow, everything queued behind it waits, which is head-of-line blocking: the one at the front of the line holds up the line. Clients work around it by opening several connections and spreading requests across them, which spends handshakes and connection slots to buy parallelism.

HTTP/2 keeps the one connection and removes the rule. It splits every request and response into small frames, each labelled with a stream number, and sends them interleaved, so that many requests and responses are in flight on the same connection at once and each finishes when it is ready. That is multiplexing: many conversations sharing one connection without waiting for one another. The connection is opened once, with one TCP handshake and one TLS handshake, and then kept for as long as both ends like, which is often hours.

There was one line left to block on, and it was TCP's. TCP is registered post: every byte is numbered and delivered in order, so if one packet is lost, the receiver holds everything that arrived after it until the resend comes, even frames of streams that had nothing to do with the loss. QUIC is a transport built on top of UDP that numbers each stream separately, so a lost packet delays only the stream it belonged to. It carries TLS inside itself, so a new connection needs one round trip and a resumed one needs none, and it names connections by an identifier rather than by addresses and ports, so a phone that walks from Wi-Fi to mobile keeps its connection. HTTP/3 is HTTP on QUIC, and it is what your browser speaks to most large sites today.

Two names ride on these. gRPC is a way for services to call each other, built on HTTP/2 streams, and is what many clusters use between pods. A WebSocket is an HTTP connection upgraded into a plain two-way channel that stays open for as long as a chat window needs it. Both are long-lived by design.

HTTP/1.1 HTTP/2 HTTP/3
Transport TCP TCP QUIC on UDP
Requests in flight per connection one at a time many many
Held up by one slow response yes no no
Held up by one lost packet yes yes that stream only

All of this shares one consequence. A connection is made to an address, not to a name. The name is looked up once, when the connection is opened, and never again while it stays open; chapter 11's TTL says how long an answer may be remembered, but an open connection is not remembering the answer, it is living in it. Change the name's answer and nothing happens to any connection already open. The change arrives at the pace of connections closing, which, for a pooled HTTP/2 client, can be a day.

Remember it as: An open connection is a conversation already in progress: it never asks directory enquiries again.

That is Friday evening's shape. Pods with old pooled connections kept talking to Paystream's public address along the old path and paid people; every new connection asked the name, got 10.20.4.31, and waited for a reply that never came. Failures grew as pools turned over, and at 17:30 the restart closed every old connection at once and turned a third into four fifths.

⚠Where it breaks
  • Long-lived connections hiding a change: a DNS or routing change rolls out as connections happen to close, so old clients keep working and new ones fail, and the failure looks random. The sign is a failure rate that tracks process age rather than code version. Know the pool's lifetime, roll a change by restarting one client and watching, and set a maximum connection age so the pool asks the name again on a schedule.
  • Head-of-line blocking on a lossy link: HTTP/2 on a bad Wi-Fi link can be slower than HTTP/1.1 with six connections, because one lost packet stalls every stream. The sign is a page that loads in bursts after pauses. HTTP/3 removes it; so does keeping connections short on links you know are poor.
  • One connection, one backend: an L4 balancer spreads connections, not requests, so an HTTP/2 or gRPC client that opens one connection sends everything down it to one pod. The sign is one hot pod and forty idle ones. Balance at L7, or let the client open a connection to each backend and spread requests itself.
  • A restart as the fix: "restart it to clear it" closes every connection at once, so any change those connections were sheltering from lands on all of them in the same second. The sign is a failure rate that jumps right after the restart. Restart one, watch, and only then the rest.

…but

The old connections had gone out through the NAT gateway wearing the node's address. The new ones went to an address inside the VPC, so the NAT gateway never touched them, and the endpoint saw each pod as itself. Nadia realised she had never asked what a pod's own address was, or where it came from, and opened the VPC's page to read it from the top.

The problem

Lunch was sandwiches eaten over keyboards. By 14:00 the HTTP/2 explanation had been written up in the channel, the 17:30 restart had a line in the timeline that no longer needed a question mark, and Sam had gone quiet, which Nadia had learned meant he was with the CEO.

She was still on the VPN and still in the platform account's console. On Friday night she had chased a single address through it. Now she wanted the whole shape. She found the VPC and listed its subnets.

kettle-nodes-a   10.0.1.0/24   zone a     kettle-endpoints-a   10.20.4.0/24   zone a
kettle-nodes-b   10.0.2.0/24   zone b     kettle-endpoints-b   10.20.5.0/24   zone b
kettle-nodes-c   10.0.3.0/24   zone c     kettle-endpoints-c   10.20.6.0/24   zone c

Three zones, and in each zone a subnet for the nodes, a smaller one for shared endpoints, and, further down the list, a public one for the load balancer. 10.20.4.31 sat in the first endpoint subnet, which agreed with Friday's route table. It was the first tidy thing she had seen all weekend.

Ruth, on the video call with her mug, looked at the shared screen. "One per building, one per job. We called those VLANs."

"Buildings?"

"Zones are buildings. Separate power, separate floors full of switches." Ruth paused. "What's above the subnets?"

Nadia clicked up a level to the VPC itself, and found the list of address blocks it owned.

kettle-prod   10.0.0.0/16   10.20.0.0/16   100.64.0.0/16

She had known about the first block since her first week. She had found the second on Friday night. Nobody had ever mentioned the third. She had filtered the subnet list by the name "kettle-", and when she took the filter off, three more subnets appeared inside 100.64, one per zone, created a year ago, with names that told her nothing.

"That's shared address space," said Ruth. "The range the ISPs were given for the insides of their big NATs. Odd thing to find in a VPC."

Nadia wrote 100.64.0.0/16: why? in the notebook and boxed it.

"Later," said Ruth. "Understand the subnets first. The cloud copied them from something, and I built the something."

◷Back then

Ruth built her data centre in the middle of the 2000s, and the first thing it taught her, she said, was that a server room is not a data centre. A server room is a cupboard that got out of hand. A data centre is a building designed around the racks: a raised floor with cold air underneath, two power feeds, and more switches than she had owned in her whole career at the ISP.

In the first month a contractor plugged a patch lead into two ports of the same switch. Nothing refused it. A switch floods a broadcast to every port, so one broadcast went round the loop, came back, and went round again, and within seconds every switch on the floor was forwarding copies of the same frame. The floor went dark without a single cable failing. She drove in at three in the morning to pull one lead.

The cure was older than her data centre. In 1985 Radia Perlman, then at Digital Equipment Corporation, had published an algorithm that let bridges discover loops among themselves and switch off the extra links until one was needed. She wrote the algorithm up as a short poem as well as a paper, and Ruth kept a copy of the poem on the wall of the network room, because it was easier to explain than the standard.

The second lesson came as the floor filled. Two thousand machines on one network meant two thousand machines hearing every shout of "who has this address?". In 1998 the IEEE had standardised 802.1Q, a four-byte tag inside the Ethernet frame carrying a twelve-bit number, so that one set of switches could carry up to 4094 separate networks that never heard each other. Ruth drew her floor as rounds: web servers in one, databases in another, management in a third.

The third lesson came last. Her network was a tree, built for traffic that came in from the internet and went back out. By the end of the decade most of her traffic went sideways, web server to cache to database, and the trunk of the tree was the bottleneck, with half its links switched off by Perlman's algorithm. A vendor engineer handed her a paper from 1953, in which Charles Clos of Bell Labs had shown how to build a telephone exchange out of small switches arranged in stages so that no call could ever block another. The data centre, Ruth said, was a telephone exchange that had forgotten its own history.

The idea

A data centre is a building that exists to hold computers, and the network inside it is designed for the opposite of the internet: short distances, enormous volumes, and one owner.

The switches from chapter 6 are the bricks. A switch learns which MAC address lives on which port and forwards each frame to that port alone. When it does not know, it floods the frame to every port, and when the frame is a broadcast it floods on purpose. Two switches with two cables between them form a loop, and a flooded frame goes round a loop forever. Spanning tree is the protocol that stops this: the switches elect one of themselves as the root and switch off any link that would make a second path, leaving a tree. The spare links come back only when a live one fails. It keeps the network up and wastes half the cables.

A VLAN, a virtual LAN, lets one set of switches behave as several unconnected ones. Each port belongs to a numbered VLAN, and frames from one VLAN are never forwarded to a port in another. Between switches, a trunk carries every VLAN on one cable by adding the 802.1Q tag to each frame on the way in and stripping it on the way out. To get from one VLAN to another a frame must go through a router, which is where you put the rules about who may talk to whom. In the postal picture, VLANs are separate post rounds sharing one building: the same corridors, different sacks, and a sorting office between them.

For twenty years the standard shape was the three-tier network: an access switch at the top of each rack, a distribution switch for each row that joins the racks and holds the VLAN routing, and a core pair that joins the rows and faces the internet. Traffic that enters from outside and goes to a server is called north-south, because that is how it runs on the diagram. Traffic between two servers inside the building is east-west.

The tree suits north-south traffic and punishes east-west. A web server talking to a database two racks away sends every frame up through the distribution and core and back down, over links shared with everyone, half of which spanning tree has switched off.

Spine-leaf is Clos's exchange rebuilt in Ethernet. Every rack has a leaf switch. Every leaf connects to every spine switch, and nothing else connects to the spines. Any server reaches any other in exactly three hops, leaf to spine to leaf, and because the links between tiers are routed rather than bridged, all of them carry traffic at once and nothing is switched off. To add capacity you add a spine. VLANs stop at the leaf, which is why the data centre later needed a way to stretch a network across a routed fabric, and that is the next chapter.

Remember it as: a data centre is a tree that grew sideways: VLANs split one building into rounds, spine-leaf gives every rack an equal road.

Kettle's subnets are VLANs with the wiring removed. One per zone, one per job, and a router between them that Nadia cannot see. The question that mattered on Saturday was the same one Ruth's VLANs had always raised: who is allowed to cross from one round to another, and who decides.

⚠Where it breaks
  • Broadcast storm: a loop between switches, or a faulty card, makes one broadcast frame multiply until every link is full of copies. The sign is a whole floor going dark at once while every cable light is solid on. Spanning tree, storm-control limits on ports, and a smaller broadcast domain stop it.
  • VLAN hopping attack: a machine sends frames with an 802.1Q tag already on them, or talks the trunk protocol to a port left in its default auto-trunk setting, and lands in a VLAN it was never given. The sign is traffic from a VLAN appearing on a host that has no port in it. Disable auto-trunking, never use VLAN 1 for anything, and allow on each trunk only the VLANs it needs.
  • Oversubscribed uplinks: forty servers in a rack share one link to the row, and the link, not the servers, is the limit. The sign is slow calls between services while every machine shows low CPU. Spine-leaf, or more uplinks per leaf, fixes the shape.
  • One flat network: everything in one VLAN because segmenting was going to be done later. The sign is that a compromised printer can reach the database. Segment by job, and route between segments through something that keeps a list.

…but

Ruth's VLANs had ended at a switch she could touch. Kettle's subnets ended at nothing Nadia could point to, and the router between them, the one that was supposed to hold the list, did not seem to exist anywhere either. If there was no box in the path, what had dropped the pod's packet?

The problem

At 15:00 Nadia went looking for the box.

If the subnets were VLANs, something sat between them and held the list. On Ruth's floor it had been a router with a name and a rack number. Nadia opened a shell in Friday's debug pod and traced the route to the endpoint, expecting to find whatever was dropping her packets somewhere along the way.

$ traceroute -n -q 1 10.20.4.31
 1  10.0.3.44   0.21 ms
 2  *
 3  *

One hop, the node the pod was running on, and then nothing. No router. The trail ended as if the endpoint were on the same wire as the node and had chosen not to reply.

"Where's the router?" she said.

"Same place as the switches," said Ruth. "You don't own it, so you don't see it."

"Then what's enforcing the rule? Something is dropping a SYN."

Ruth told her where to look. Nadia found the endpoint's network interface, the one with the address 10.20.4.31, and opened its details. Attached to the interface itself, not to the subnet, not to any router, was a security group: a named list of allowed traffic, which she had seen on every node without ever asking what it was. Before she could open it Sam's face appeared on the call, his phone held against his chest.

"Paystream want to know whether we are going to keep hammering them."

"Tell them it stops when we stop retrying," said Ruth, without looking up. Then, to Nadia: "Don't read the rule yet. Read where it lives. It's on the interface. There is no box. The host that interface lives on checks every packet in and out of it, and you will never log in to that host."

Nadia wrote: firewall = per interface, done by the host. Then, underneath: which host?

"Whichever one the provider put it on," said Ruth. "I learned that in the 2010s, and I'm still not sure I like it."

◷Back then

By the end of the 2000s, Ruth said, her racks had stopped being full of servers and started being full of hosts, and a host is a server that pretends to be twenty. Each one ran a hypervisor, and each hypervisor ran virtual machines that believed they had a network card. The card was software. The cable it plugged into was software. The switch at the other end of the cable was a virtual switch inside the host, and for the first time in her career there was a switch on her network that she could not walk up to.

Her VLAN tags had to follow the machines inside. When a virtual machine moved from one host to another, which it now did without asking her, its VLAN had to be waiting on the new host's leaf switch, and if it was not, the machine arrived and went silent. She spent a year pre-configuring every VLAN on every leaf, which defeated the point of VLANs.

Two documents changed the shape of the problem. In April 2008 Nick McKeown of Stanford and his co-authors published OpenFlow, a protocol by which a separate controller could tell a switch what to do with each flow of packets. The switch would keep a table; the controller would fill it. They wrote it so that researchers could try ideas on the campus network without buying new switches. The industry took it and called the approach software-defined networking.

Then in August 2014 engineers from several vendors published RFC 7348, VXLAN. A frame from a virtual machine need not travel on a VLAN at all. The host could wrap it inside an ordinary UDP packet addressed to whichever host held the destination machine, send it across the routed fabric like any other packet, and the receiving host would unwrap it. The tag inside the wrapper had twenty-four bits, sixteen million networks instead of 4094, and the physical switches never knew any of them existed.

By then Ruth was moving everything to the cloud, and she realised, reading the RFC, that the providers had been doing this for years before anyone wrote it down.

The idea

Virtualisation is running several computers on one. A hypervisor is the program that does it: it owns the real processor, memory and network card, and shares them out among virtual machines, each of which sees a processor, some memory and a network card of its own. The card it sees is a virtual interface, and the hypervisor decides what happens to every frame that leaves it.

Inside the host sits a virtual switch. It behaves like the switches of chapter 6, learning which virtual interface holds which MAC address, except that it is software with a table, and the table can hold rules as well as addresses. The physical card is one of its ports; so is every virtual machine.

An overlay network is a network that exists only in those tables. The physical switches and routers form the underlay: they carry packets between hosts and know nothing else. When virtual machine A sends a frame to virtual machine B, the virtual switch on A's host looks up which host currently holds B, wraps the whole frame in a new packet addressed to that host, and sends it. B's host unwraps it and hands the original frame to B. VXLAN is the common way of wrapping: the frame goes inside a UDP packet to port 4789, with a small header carrying a twenty-four-bit VNI, the number of the virtual network it belongs to. The wrapping point on each host is a VTEP.

This is where the postal picture stops helping. The best it can offer is letters inside parcels carried by another courier, which is true as far as it goes, but it leads you to look for the courier's van, and there is none. Here is the same thing without the metaphor. A is given an address in a network that has no cables. That network is a table, copied to every host, saying which host holds which address. The cables carry only host-to-host packets. If B moves to a third host, the table changes and A's next frame goes to the new host, while A's address, B's address and the network they share have not changed at all, because none of them were ever on a wire.

Who writes the table? Software-defined networking, SDN, is the name for separating two jobs: the data plane, the hosts and switches that forward packets by consulting a table, and the control plane, a controller that decides what the tables should say and pushes it down. OpenFlow was one protocol for the pushing. Every large cloud runs a controller of its own design that knows where every virtual interface is and what it is allowed to do.

That last item is the one that matters on Saturday. In a building, the rules live in a box in the path. In an overlay there is no need for the box, because every packet already passes through a virtual switch on its way out of one interface and another on its way into the next. So the rules are attached to the interface, and the host that owns the interface applies them, on the way out and again on the way in. The firewall is everywhere and nowhere. It keeps state, like the stateful firewalls of chapter 15, so a reply is allowed if the request was. When a packet matches no rule the host drops it before the destination sees it, and nothing in the path sends a refusal.

Remember it as: the cloud's network is a table on every host, and the firewall is a rule on every interface, enforced by the host that owns it.

This is why Nadia's traceroute found one hop and then nothing, and why on Friday the SYN went out and nothing came back: the pod's packet reached the host holding 10.20.4.31, and that host compared it with the interface's list and threw it away.

⚠Where it breaks
  • Looking for the box: an engineer spends an afternoon tracing a route to find the firewall that is dropping traffic. The sign is a traceroute that ends in stars one hop out. Look at the rules on the destination interface, and at the logs the host keeps on its behalf.
  • MTU and the wrapper: VXLAN adds about fifty bytes to every frame, so a frame that was already full-size no longer fits in the underlay. The sign is small requests that work and large responses that hang, with no error anywhere. Raise the underlay MTU or lower the one the machines use.
  • Controller gone: the control plane fails, and existing flows keep working while new machines, new rules and moved machines are ignored. The sign is "everything that was running is fine, nothing new comes up". Run the controller redundantly and let the data plane forward without it.
  • Spoofed overlay packets attack: VXLAN has no authentication, so anyone who can send UDP into the underlay can forge a wrapped frame into any VNI. The sign is frames appearing in a virtual network from a host that has no machines in it. Keep the underlay unreachable from tenants, filter the VXLAN port at the edge, and have hosts refuse wrappers from unknown VTEPs.

…but

If every interface carried its own guard, the question was no longer "where is the firewall" but "how many interfaces, and which rules on each". Nadia could not answer, because in eight months she had never once drawn Kettle's VPC. She turned to a clean page.

The problem

If the guard stood at every network interface, Ruth had said, then the question was not "where is the firewall" but "which interface, in which subnet, with which rules". At 15:40 on Saturday Nadia realised she could not answer the middle part. She had been typing 10.0.0.0/16 into forms for eight months and had never once drawn the thing it described.

She was still on the company VPN, looking at the platform account's console, which Jonas had built and nobody else had ever needed to open. She turned to a clean page in the notebook and wrote Kettle VPC at the top.

Three address blocks were attached to it. 10.0.0.0/16, the one everybody used. 10.20.0.0/16, which the console called shared-endpoints. And 100.64.0.0/16, which she had found an hour earlier and still could not place.

Under them, subnets, in threes. Three zones, named a, b and c. Each zone had a public subnet with a leg of the load balancer in it, a private subnet with the cluster's nodes in it, an endpoint subnet carved from 10.20.0.0/16, and a subnet from 100.64.0.0/16 called only cluster-secondary, which told her nothing. Twelve subnets. She drew twelve boxes and ran out of page by the third column.

Then the route tables. The one attached to the private subnets read:

10.0.0.0/16      local
10.20.0.0/16     local
100.64.0.0/16    local
0.0.0.0/0        nat-gateway-a

The table on the public subnets was the same except for the last line, which pointed at something called the internet gateway. The table on the endpoint subnets had no last line at all. She drew arrows. At 16:00 she held the page up to the camera.

"That," said Ruth, "is the first time anyone at Kettle has drawn it. Keep it. You'll be looking at it all evening."

◷Back then

Ruth had been halfway through building a data centre when, in August 2006, a colleague called Dev wheeled his chair over and showed her a web page where you could rent a computer by the hour. It was the beta of Amazon's EC2, the Elastic Compute Cloud, and Dev had rented one over lunch. Ruth was not impressed. She had spent four months getting power and cooling into a room in Slough, and here was a machine that existed in ninety seconds and cost ten cents.

What struck her, when she looked properly, was the network. The rented machine had a public address, straight on to the internet. Every rented machine did. There were no subnets to design, no routers to configure and no cupboard to put them in. There was a list of allowed ports, and that was the whole of the network, and that was the point. The early cloud was flat: one shared network, every machine facing the street.

For a company like Ruth's, that was a problem. Her databases had never had public addresses and were not going to start. Her auditors wanted to see a boundary. Her applications assumed private address ranges, two tiers and a firewall between them, which is what everyone had built since the nineties.

In August 2009 Amazon announced the Virtual Private Cloud. You chose an address block. You cut it into subnets. You wrote route tables. You decided which subnets could reach the internet and which could not. Nothing you put inside could be reached from outside unless you built the door yourself. It was, Ruth said, the moment the cloud stopped being a place where you rented a machine and became a place you could move a network to. She did not move hers for another five years, but she started planning the address blocks that autumn, on paper, and the plan she drew then is the shape of every VPC she has built since.

"Draw it before you build it," she told Nadia. "Addresses are the one thing you can't change later without moving house."

The idea

A VPC (AWS: VPC; Azure: virtual network, VNet) is a private network that you define inside a cloud provider's building: a gated estate you rent inside a city you don't own. Nothing is inside it until you put something there, and nothing can reach it until you build a way in.

The first decision is the address block, written as a CIDR prefix from chapter 9. 10.0.0.0/16 gives 65,536 addresses. Choose it from the private ranges of chapter 14, choose it large, and choose a block that nothing else you own uses, because one day you will want to connect this network to another, and two networks with the same addresses cannot be told apart. A VPC can carry more than one block. Kettle's 10.0.0.0/16 was chosen in a hurry; the second and third blocks were added later, when the first ran short, and the route tables learned about them with no help from anyone.

Inside the block you cut subnets, smaller prefixes such as 10.0.1.0/24. Each subnet lives in exactly one availability zone (AWS: Availability Zone; Azure: availability zone): a separate building with its own power and cooling, close enough to the others for fast links and far enough that a fire in one does not take out the rest. That is why Kettle's subnets come in threes. One of each kind in each zone, so that losing a zone loses a third of the capacity and none of the services.

A subnet is not public or private by nature. It is public or private by its route table (AWS: route table; Azure: route table, or user-defined routes): the sorting office's pigeonholes from chapter 12, now a short list you write yourself and attach to each subnet. Every table begins with a local route, meaning that every block attached to the VPC is reachable directly, without leaving. That one line is why 10.20.4.31 was reachable from the nodes the moment it existed.

A public subnet is one whose table sends 0.0.0.0/0, everything else, to an internet gateway (AWS: internet gateway; Azure: no separate object, outbound access is built in or set by a NAT gateway): the door between the estate and the city. Machines in a public subnet can be given a public address and be reached from the internet. Kettle's load balancer lives there. A private subnet has no such route. Its machines have private addresses only, and nothing on the internet can start a conversation with them. Kettle's nodes live there. When a private machine needs to reach out, for a software update or a payment, its table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway (AWS: NAT gateway; Azure: NAT Gateway): the company post room from chapter 14, sitting in a public subnet, swapping the private address for one public address and remembering who asked. Replies come back through it. Fresh conversations from outside do not.

The three kinds of subnet differ in one line of one table each.

Subnet The three Kettle blocks 0.0.0.0/0
Public local internet gateway
Private local NAT gateway in the same zone
Endpoint local no route

A packet leaving a node to a public address follows the private table to the end: not local, so out through the NAT gateway, then the internet gateway, then the city.

Remember it as: A VPC is an estate you rent inside someone's city: you choose the postcodes, write the pigeonholes, and build every gate yourself.

That sequence is the path every call to Paystream took until Friday. Since 15:58 the destination has been 10.20.4.31, which matches the second line of every table, local, so the packet never reaches the NAT gateway or the internet gateway at all. It goes straight to the endpoint interface, and straight into whatever guard stands at it.

⚠Where it breaks
  • Overlapping address blocks: two networks each chosen as 10.0.0.0/16 work perfectly alone and can never be joined; the sign is a request to connect them refused for overlapping ranges. Plan every block across the whole company before the first VPC exists, and write the plan down.
  • Private subnet with no way out: the table has no 0.0.0.0/0 route, or its NAT gateway sits in a zone that has failed; the sign is updates and outside API calls hanging in one zone and working in the others. One NAT gateway per zone, and a route table per zone to match.
  • Accidentally public: a route to the internet gateway on the wrong table, plus a public address, puts a database on the street; the sign is a scanner finding port 5432 from outside. Keep public subnets for things that must face the internet, and give nothing else a public address.
  • Running out of houses, again: a /24 holds 251 usable addresses, and a cluster that hands out addresses faster than anyone planned eats them in a week; the sign is "no free addresses" when something scales. Size subnets for the number of things that will get addresses, not the number of machines, which is why Kettle grew a block it then forgot about.

…but

The endpoint interface sat in a subnet whose only route was local. Nothing in the drawing could lose a packet on the way there. Only the guard at the interface could, and a guard who keeps no record is half a guard. Ruth asked whether the platform account had flow logs turned on.

The problem

Flow logs were not on. Jonas had never needed them. Nadia ate a sandwich at the kitchen table, copied the drawing out again more neatly, and at 17:35 turned on flow logs for the endpoint's three network interfaces. The console told her, in the unhurried way of consoles, that records would start to appear in about ten minutes.

While she waited she opened the security group on the endpoint. Jonas had written it on Friday. It had one inbound rule.

Inbound   TCP 443   from 10.0.0.0/16    "kettle nodes"
Outbound  all       to 0.0.0.0/0        (default)

Nodes lived in 10.0.0.0/16. Jonas had tested from a node. The rule was correct for the test. She ran the same connection check from a node herself, so that at least one line in the log would be hers.

The first records arrived at 17:58. Her test was there, 10.0.2.14 to 10.20.4.31, port 443, ACCEPT. Everything else was not hers.

100.64.3.17    10.20.4.31  443  TCP  REJECT
100.64.5.102   10.20.4.31  443  TCP  REJECT
100.64.3.17    10.20.4.31  443  TCP  REJECT

Pages of it. Every rejected line came from an address beginning 100.64. The rule allowed 10.0.0.0/16 and mentioned nothing else. She laid the rule next to the log and, at 18:00, wrote under both of them: What is 100.64? Who lives there?

"Now you've seen the drop," said Ruth. "Chapter seven's missing reply, written down by the thing that dropped it. Before you fix the rule, you need to know which kind of guard wrote it."

◷Back then

Ruth's data centre had a boundary router with an access list on it, an ordered list of lines that said permit or deny, read top to bottom, first match wins. In 2003 she added a line to let the world reach the new web tier on port 80, tested it from her desk, and saw nothing. The request went in. The reply never came out.

Dev found it, eventually, with a packet capture. The reply from the web server was addressed to her laptop's high-numbered port, the ephemeral port from chapter 7, and no line in the list permitted traffic to high-numbered ports. The list had no memory. It did not know that this packet was the second half of a conversation it had allowed a moment ago. Each packet stood alone and was judged alone. She added a line for the return path, felt foolish, and kept the capture as a reminder.

Firewalls that remembered conversations already existed by then, and her data centre got one. It kept a table of connections it had allowed, and let replies through on the strength of that table. The guard at the boundary now had a notebook.

When EC2 arrived in 2006, the only network control it offered was a list of allowed ports attached to each rented machine, and that list remembered conversations from the first day. There was no boundary to put a checkpoint on, because there was no boundary. When the VPC came three years later, the boundary came back, and so did the old stateless list, as an option, at the subnet's edge, for the people whose auditors wanted a checkpoint at the district line as well as a guard at each door. Ruth had been one of those people. "Two guards," she told Nadia. "One with a notebook, one without. Most outages at a cloud boundary come from forgetting which is which."

The idea

A security group (AWS: security group; Azure: network security group) is a guard for each flat. It is attached to a network interface, not to a subnet, and it travels with the interface. Its rules say only what is allowed: port, protocol, and where from. There is no deny line. Anything no rule allows is dropped, silently, with no refusal sent back, which is why checkout saw a timeout and not an error. A security group is stateful: it remembers each conversation it lets in, and lets the replies out without a rule for them, and the same the other way round.

A network ACL (AWS: network ACL; Azure: NSG rules on a subnet; there is no separate stateless list) is the checkpoint at the district boundary. It is attached to a subnet and checks every packet crossing in or out. Its rules are numbered and read in order, and they can say deny as well as allow. It is stateless: it keeps no notebook, so each packet is judged alone, and a reply needs its own rule covering the ephemeral ports it will be addressed to. By default it allows everything, which is why most people never notice it.

Both apply to the same packet. A packet from one subnet to an interface in another crosses the first subnet's checkpoint on the way out, the second subnet's checkpoint on the way in, and then meets the security group at the door.

Security group Network ACL
Attached to a network interface a subnet
Rules allow only allow and deny, numbered
Memory stateful: replies follow stateless: replies need a rule
No match dropped silently depends on the last rule

Flow logs (AWS: VPC Flow Logs; Azure: VNet flow logs) are the record that neither guard keeps on its own. Turned on for an interface, a subnet or a whole VPC, they write one line per conversation: source, destination, port, protocol, how many packets, and whether the host let it through or not. They hold no payload, they arrive a few minutes late, and they do not say which of the two guards made the decision. They are still the only way to see a silent drop without a capture at both ends.

Two habits decide whether these guards help or hurt. The first is the source. A rule can allow a range, from 10.0.0.0/16, or it can allow a group: anything whose own security group is the one named. A rule that says allow 443 from the cluster's group follows the machines wherever their addresses go. A rule that says from 10.0.0.0/16 follows the addresses, and trusts anything that has one. The second habit is 0.0.0.0/0. It means from anywhere, it is what the tutorial said to type, and it turns the guard into a doorstop.

Remember it as: Security group: a guard per flat, remembers who it let in. Network ACL: a checkpoint at the district boundary, no memory, both ways.

The endpoint's guard had one line, and the packets from 100.64 matched none of it. Allow-only means no match is a silent drop, and a silent drop at the far end is a SYN that gets nothing back: the capture from chapter 7, finally explained from the other side.

⚠Where it breaks
  • The 0.0.0.0/0 habit attack: a rule written as from anywhere to make a test pass is left in place, and a scanner finds the port within the hour; the sign is a login prompt or a database handshake reachable from a coffee shop. Allow from a group or a named range, never from everywhere, and review every rule that says 0.0.0.0/0 on an inbound line.
  • Stateless rule missing the return path: a network ACL allows the request in but has no line for the reply's ephemeral port, so the handshake never completes; the sign is a request that reaches the server and a client that times out. Add the return rule for the high ports, or leave the ACL open and do the real work in security groups.
  • Two guards, one forgotten: the security group is right and the packet is still dropped, because a network ACL on the subnet denies it; the sign is a REJECT in the flow log that no security group rule explains. Check both lists, in both directions, in both subnets.
  • Silent drop read as a network fault: a timeout is blamed on routing or the provider, because nobody refused anything; the sign is a route table that says local and a connection that never opens. A timeout to an address inside the VPC is a guard until proven otherwise.
  • Flow logs read too soon: the log is empty because it was turned on a minute ago, and the conclusion is "no traffic"; the sign is a gap that ends exactly when the records start. Wait ten minutes, then filter by interface and by REJECT.

…but

"I could widen it," Nadia said. "Allow 100.64.0.0/16 as well." "You could," said Ruth. "Do you know what you'd be letting in?" She did not. And there was a harder question under that one, which Sam rejoined the call at 18:40 to ask on the CEO's behalf: why had Jonas needed a private letterbox at all?

Chapter 27 · Act VIConnecting the Islands#

The problem

Sam's question, which was the CEO's question, was whether they could roll Jonas's change back. Nadia had thought about it. Deleting the endpoint would put api.paystream.example back to its public addresses, and the old path through the NAT gateway was still there in every route table. It would probably work. Probably was doing the same work the question mark had done on Friday.

"Before you do that," said Ruth, "tell me why he built it."

Nadia had the ticket from a month ago. During the September sale the NAT gateway in zone a had run out of ports, and the graph Jonas had attached to the ticket still looked like a cliff.

nat-gateway-a   ErrorPortAllocation     peak 1,412 per minute   14 Sept 19:02
nat-gateway-a   BytesOutToDestination   2.1 TB                  September

Two terabytes of payment traffic out through the post room, every byte of it charged, and on the busiest evening of the year the post room had run out of envelopes.

Ruth held up her tablet to the camera and drew an island. "Kettle's VPC. Draw me every way off it."

Nadia drew the internet gateway and the NAT gateway, because those were on her page. Ruth drew the rest: a link to another estate, a hub with many spokes, a sealed pouch through the public post, a private road, and a letterbox. By 19:00 there were six ways off the island, and Nadia had written Jonas's name under the letterbox.

"He chose well," said Ruth. "That's what makes this annoying."

◷Back then

Ruth moved her data centre to the cloud in 2014, and she did it the way everyone did: one VPC per team, so that nobody could tread on anybody else. By 2017 there were thirty-one of them, and the teams had started to need each other.

The tool for that was peering, a direct link between two VPCs. It worked, and it did not carry through: if finance was peered to billing and billing to the warehouse, finance could still not reach the warehouse. Every pair that needed to talk needed its own link. Ruth kept the links in a spreadsheet. The spreadsheet reached four hundred rows, and the diagram on the wall that went with it was known, not fondly, as the hairball. A VPN tunnel from the office in Reading joined one of the VPCs, and a dedicated line, ordered in the spring and delivered in the autumn, joined another, and neither could be reached from most of the rest.

In November 2017 Amazon announced PrivateLink. A service in somebody else's VPC, including another company's, could be reached through a network interface that appeared in your own subnet, with an address from your own block. No peering, no shared routes, no overlapping-address problem, and the other side never saw your network at all. Ruth's first use of it was for a payment provider, which she found funny on Saturday and did not say.

In November 2018 came the Transit Gateway: one hub that every VPC, every VPN and every dedicated line attached to, with one set of routes between them. It did for her estates what a sorting office had always done for streets. The hairball came down off the wall in a week. "Thirty-one islands," she told Nadia, "and I'd spent a year building bridges. What I needed was a post office."

The idea

A VPC is an island. Sooner or later something on it needs something off it, and there are only a few kinds of crossing.

Peering (AWS: VPC peering; Azure: VNet peering) joins two VPCs directly. Each side adds a route for the other's block, and traffic passes between them on the provider's own network, never on the internet. Two rules follow from how it is built. The blocks must not overlap, because a router cannot tell two 10.0.1.14s apart. And it is not transitive: a link from A to B and a link from B to C does not give A a path to C.

A transit hub (AWS: Transit Gateway; Azure: Virtual WAN hub) is a router you attach islands to. Each VPC gets one link to the hub, the hub holds one route table, and anything attached can reach anything else the table allows. Ten VPCs peered in pairs need forty-five links; ten VPCs on a hub need ten.

Hybrid connectivity is the crossing to premises you own. The cheap way is a VPN (AWS: Site-to-Site VPN; Azure: VPN Gateway), the sealed pouch of chapter 18, carried over the public internet between your office router and a gateway in the cloud. The expensive way is a dedicated line (AWS: Direct Connect; Azure: ExpressRoute): a physical circuit from your building to the provider's edge, with predictable latency and a predictable bill, ordered in months. Both usually land on the transit hub.

A private endpoint (AWS: interface VPC endpoint, PrivateLink; Azure: private endpoint, Private Link) is the odd one out, because it is not a crossing at all. It is a private letterbox for an outside company, installed inside your estate. The provider puts its service behind a load balancer in its own VPC and offers it as a private link. You create an endpoint for it, and a network interface appears in a subnet of your choosing, with an address from your block, in each zone you ask for. Packets to that address are carried to the provider's service on the provider's network. The provider never learns your routes, cannot start a conversation back, and does not need your address block to differ from anyone else's. With private DNS turned on, the service's public name resolves inside your VPC to the endpoint's addresses, which is the split answer Nadia found in chapter 11.

The last decision is egress: what leaves the island, by which door, and whether it needs to leave at all. A NAT gateway has about 55,000 ports per public address for each destination, and charges for every gigabyte. When one destination takes most of the traffic, every port and every gigabyte of it is spent on a path that leaves the provider's network only to come back in. An endpoint to that destination removes it from egress entirely.

Remember it as: Peering joins two estates, a hub is one sorting office for many, a private letterbox serves an outside company: three ways off the island.

That is why Jonas was right. The endpoint took the heaviest destination off the NAT gateway, ended the port exhaustion, cut the bill, and kept payment traffic off the public internet. What he could have done differently was smaller: leave private DNS off and move callers one at a time; test from where the traffic really comes from, not from a node; and write the rule on the letterbox to name the callers rather than the street they stood in. The letterbox was right. The list on its door was not.

⚠Where it breaks
  • Peering that does not carry through: A is peered to B and B to C, and A cannot reach C; the sign is a route that exists on paper and a timeout in practice. Peer directly, or put the islands on a transit hub and let one route table do the work.
  • Private endpoint is one way: the provider cannot call you back through it, so webhooks and callbacks still arrive over the internet; the sign is outbound calls working and inbound notifications silently stopping. Keep a public path for anything the provider sends to you, and know which direction each integration runs.
  • Private DNS flipped all at once: turning private DNS on moves every caller in the VPC as their caches expire, with no way to move one caller first; the sign is a partial failure that grows over an hour. Test reachability against the endpoint's own addresses from the real callers before the name is switched.
  • Hybrid line with no second path: one dedicated line from the office, and a digger finds it; the sign is the whole premises vanishing from the hub at once. A VPN over the internet as the standby, tested by pulling the main line on purpose.
  • Egress by accident: everything leaves through one NAT gateway, and a sale fills its ports; the sign is ErrorPortAllocation climbing with the order rate. Endpoints for the heavy destinations, a NAT gateway in each zone, and a written list of what is allowed to leave at all.

…but

"So the letterbox was right," Nadia said, "and the door was right, and the list on the door was wrong." Ruth nodded. "The list trusted an address range. That is the oldest mistake in the trade, and it has had a name for twenty years."

Chapter 28 · Act VINever Trust the Inside#
