The problem

At 19:30 Nadia wrote the whole thing out as one sentence, because Ruth had taught her on Friday that you cannot debug what you cannot name. The rule allows 443 from 10.0.0.0/16 because the nodes live there. The rejected packets come from 100.64.0.0/16. The rule trusted a range of addresses, and whatever is calling the letterbox does not stand in that range.

"Now say what the rule should have said," said Ruth.

"Allow checkout."

"Not allow anything standing in the right street. Allow checkout. Identity, not address." Ruth put her mug down. "That is zero trust in one sentence. People have written whole books trying to say it more slowly."

Sam, still on the call, asked the reasonable thing. "Can we add 100.64 to the rule and go home?"

"When you can tell me what 100.64 is," said Ruth, "yes. Adding an address range you can't name is how this started."

Nadia went back to the flow log and grouped the rejected lines by source.

rejected sources, last 30 min:   39 distinct
all within:                      100.64.0.0/16
accepted sources:                10.0.2.14  (her own test)

Thirty-nine addresses, all in the block nobody had mentioned, all trying to reach the letterbox on 443, all turned away by a rule that had been right for the one test anyone had run. She wrote 39 in the margin and did not yet know why the number bothered her.

◷Back then

Ruth built her data centre with a hard shell. A firewall pair at the boundary, a DMZ from chapter 15, and inside it a flat, trusting network where any machine could talk to any other, because they were all inside. In 2004 she read about a group calling itself the Jericho Forum: security officers from large companies, many of them British, meeting under the Open Group, arguing that the wall was already gone. Laptops left the building every evening. Partners had tunnels in. Applications talked to other companies' applications over the web. They called the trend de-perimeterisation, which was an ugly word for a true thing. Ruth thought they were right, and did nothing about it for years, because her auditors liked walls and so, if she was honest, did she.

In 2010 John Kindervag, an analyst at Forrester, published a paper under the title "No More Chewy Centers". The picture was of a sweet with a hard shell and a soft inside: every effort spent on the boundary, and nothing to stop someone who got past it. His argument, as Ruth retold it, was that the trust itself was the flaw. A packet should not be believed because of where it came from. He called the alternative zero trust, and summed it up in a phrase that has been on slides ever since: never trust, always verify.

The proof that it could be done at scale came in December 2014, in an article by Rory Ward and Betsy Beyer in the magazine ;login:, describing a programme at Google called BeyondCorp. After an intrusion into its network, Google had set out to remove the privilege of being inside. Employees would reach internal applications from anywhere, with no VPN, and every request would be judged on who the user was and what state their device was in. Being on the corporate network bought you nothing. "That was when I believed it," Ruth said. "Not because of the idea. Because someone had done the work."

The idea

Segmentation is cutting a network into parts with a guard between them. The VLANs of chapter 23, the subnets and network ACLs of chapter 26 and the DMZ of chapter 15 are all segmentation. It limits how far a mistake or an intruder can travel. Its weakness is the size of the parts: inside one segment, everything still trusts everything.

Micro-segmentation shrinks the parts until each is one workload. The guard moves from the boundary to every door: a security group on every network interface, and, inside a cluster, a policy on every pod, which chapter 30 will come to. Two machines in the same subnet must still be allowed to talk. The flat inside is gone.

Zero trust is the principle that makes micro-segmentation worth the effort. No request is trusted because of where it comes from. Each one is checked for who is asking, what they are asking for, and whether the asker is in a fit state, and that check happens whether the request comes from the internet or from the next rack. The network location is not a credential.

At the network level, zero trust comes down to one question at each door: where are you from, or who are you. An address answers the first. It says which street a packet stood in when it was sent, and that is all it says. Addresses are reused, translated by NAT, carried through overlays, and forged by anyone who can write a packet header. An identity answers the second: a group the sender's interface belongs to, a certificate the sender holds, a role the platform has issued. Identity follows the workload when its address changes, and an address range follows whoever happens to be standing in it.

The rule trusts Example at Kettle Breaks when
An address range from 10.0.0.0/16 callers move, NAT hides them, an intruder is inside
A group from the cluster's security group the group is given to the wrong thing
A workload identity checkout's certificate, checked by both sides the key leaks, which is what rotation is for

The last row is where the network hands over to cryptography and identity, which is the subject of chapter 31 and, in depth, of Cybersecurity: The Keep. The middle row is available today, in the console, as a security group rule. Providers also let a rule name a role instead of a network at all, as an identity-based policy (AWS: IAM policy on the endpoint; Azure: role-based access control), which is the same idea one layer up.

Remember it as: Every door checks your badge, even inside the building: an address says where you stood, not who you are.

Kettle's rule said anything from 10.0.0.0/16 may come in, because the nodes lived there and the test had come from a node. It was a rule about a street. The callers had a name, and the rule never asked for it.

⚠Where it breaks
  • Lateral movement attack: an attacker who lands on one machine inside the shell walks sideways to the others, because inside is trusted; the sign is connections between machines that have no business talking, often at night. Segment, put a guard on every interface, and require identity for every connection, so that one lost laptop is one lost laptop.
  • Rule by address range: a rule allows a block because the right things lived there on the day it was written; the sign is a rule that was correct for one test and a timeout from everything the test did not cover. Reference the callers' group or identity, and treat any inbound rule written as a range as a question to be answered.
  • Hard shell, chewy centre: all the money goes on the boundary and the inside is flat; the sign is one phished account reaching the database in an afternoon. Micro-segmentation, and the assumption in every design review that the boundary has already been crossed.
  • Zero trust bought in a box: a product with the words on the tin is placed in front of a network that has not changed; the sign is the phrase in the slides and 0.0.0.0/0 in the rules. Zero trust is a design, not a purchase, and it is finished when the rules name identities.

…but

Thirty-nine sources. Forty-one checkout pods. She had been looking at the two numbers for a full minute before she let herself put them next to each other. "Ruth," she said at 20:50, "what address does a pod actually have?" Ruth smiled for the first time since Friday. "Go and look. From inside one."

The problem

At 21:00 Nadia did as she was told and went to look from inside one. She opened a shell in the debug pod she had used for Friday's capture and asked it what address it had.

$ ip -4 addr show eth0
    inet 100.64.3.17/16 scope global eth0

It was the pod. The pod she was sitting in had the address the endpoint was throwing away. Not a node, not a gateway. Pods got their addresses from the second block, and thirty-nine of the forty-one checkout pods had tried the letterbox in the last half hour. The other two, she guessed, had not been handed a card payment in the last half hour.

"Jonas tested it," she said. "It's in the change. A quick connection check."

"From where?" said Ruth.

Nadia read the change again. Tested from a node. Her own test earlier, from 10.0.2.14, had been from a node too. She asked a node and a pod the same question.

node$ nc -zv -w 3 10.20.4.31 443
Connection to 10.20.4.31 443 port succeeded
pod$  nc -zv -w 3 10.20.4.31 443
nc: connect to 10.20.4.31 port 443 (tcp) timed out

The node lived in 10.0.0.0/16, so the guard let it in. The pod did not. And on the old path, out through the NAT gateway, the pod's address had been rewritten to the node's before anything beyond the VPC could see it. Until Friday, no 100.64 address had ever reached that guard.

She typed it into the channel at 21:31 in three lines: pods use the secondary CIDR; traffic that stays inside the VPC keeps the pod's address; the endpoint's rule allows only node addresses. "That's what 100.64 is," she added, for Ruth. Sam replied "Do it." At 21:41 she widened the rule to include 100.64.0.0/16. At 21:44 the first new connection from a checkout pod to 10.20.4.31 finished its handshake. At 21:47 the success line on the dashboard, which had sat at a fifth since the restart, climbed to all of it and stayed there.

Ruth said nothing for a moment. Then: "Write down the time. You'll want it on Monday."

◷Back then

The first container Ruth ever saw on a network, she said, was in 2013, and it was hiding.

In March 2013 Solomon Hykes had shown Docker at a conference in a demo a few minutes long: a way to pack a program with everything it needed and run it anywhere, in seconds. By the autumn a developer at the company Ruth then worked for had one on his laptop and wanted it on a server. Ruth asked what address it would have. He did not know. Docker gave each container a private address on a virtual bridge inside the host, 172.17-something, and hid the lot behind the host's own address with NAT and a port mapping. From the network, a container was invisible. It was the host, on port 8080. Ruth recognised it at once: the company post room, built in miniature on every server. It worked for one container. It worked for ten. It stopped working when two containers both wanted port 80, or when a container on one host had to call one on another and nobody could say which host, which port, this week.

In June 2014 Google announced Kubernetes, built by Joe Beda, Brendan Burns, Craig McLuckie and others out of what Google had learned running containers on its own machines. One lesson was that juggling ports on shared host addresses makes everything harder. So the Kubernetes networking model drew a line. Every pod gets its own IP address. Every pod can reach every other pod by that address, with no NAT between them. The address a pod sees on itself is the address everyone else uses to reach it. The model said what, not how.

In 2015 engineers at CoreOS wrote a short specification, the Container Network Interface, CNI, so that an orchestrator could hand a new container to a plug-in and say "connect this", and the plug-in, whichever one it was, did the wiring. Kubernetes adopted it. Ruth said that was the part she liked. The rule was fixed. The wiring was pluggable.

The idea

A container is a process that has been told a different story about the machine it is on. One part of that story is the network. The Linux kernel can give a process its own network namespace: a private copy of the network stack, with its own interfaces, addresses and routing table, as if it were a separate machine. A pod is one network namespace shared by the containers inside it. Inside, there is an eth0 with an address that the host does not show.

To connect that private stack to anything, the plug-in makes a veth pair: a virtual cable with two ends, where whatever goes in at one end comes out of the other. One end is moved into the pod's namespace and named eth0. The other stays on the host. On a classic set-up the host ends are plugged into a bridge, a virtual switch inside the host (chapter 24), so pods on one node reach each other as if they shared a cable, and the node routes everything else on and off the machine.

The Kubernetes networking model is a rule about what this wiring must achieve, whoever does it: every pod has its own address, every pod can reach every pod by that address, and no NAT happens between them. So the address in a pod's own ip addr is the address in the other pod's logs, in the flow logs, and at the guard. Docker's picture, where a container hid behind its host, was thrown away on purpose.

CNI is the plug-in standard that does the wiring. When the node starts a pod it runs the plug-in with "add". The plug-in creates the veth pair, picks an address from the pod CIDR, the range set aside for pods, writes the routes, and reports back. On removal it is called with "delete". The plug-in also decides how pods on different nodes reach each other, and there are two families. In an overlay, each node's pod range is carried inside packets addressed to the node itself, letters inside parcels (chapter 24); the VPC never sees a pod address. In VPC-native addressing, pod addresses are real VPC addresses, attached to the node's network interfaces, and the VPC's own route table delivers them. No parcel, but every pod consumes a VPC address, and a node subnet can run dry. That happened to Kettle a year ago. The answer was custom networking: a second block is added to the VPC, pods draw their addresses from it, and nodes stay where they were. Kettle's second block is 100.64.0.0/16, a postcode district of its own, routed like any other.

One more rule finishes the picture. SNAT, source network address translation, is rewriting the sender's address on a packet as it leaves. Kettle's plug-in does it in exactly one case: when the destination is outside the VPC. The pod's 100.64 address becomes the node's 10.0 address, and the NAT gateway then turns that into a public one, because 100.64.0.0/10 is reserved for carrier-grade NAT (chapter 14) and nobody on the internet will route it back. When the destination is inside the VPC, the VPC can route 100.64 on its own, so nothing is rewritten and the packet keeps the pod's address.

Remember it as: A pod is a real address. Leaving the VPC it borrows the node's; staying inside, it keeps its own, and your rules must know that.

Put the two paths together and Friday explains itself. For a year every packet from a pod to Paystream had gone out through SNAT wearing a node address, so a rule written for 10.0.0.0/16 had always been enough. The private endpoint moved Paystream inside the VPC, SNAT stepped aside, and the guard met 100.64 for the first time. Jonas's test from a node was a true test of the wrong sender.

⚠Where it breaks
  • SNAT assumptions: a rule or a test is written as if everything from the cluster arrives as a node address, when inside the VPC it arrives as a pod address. The tell-tale is a check that passes from a node and fails from a pod, with flow logs showing a range nobody expected. Test from a pod, and allow the pod CIDR or, better, reference the cluster's own group rather than a range.
  • Pod CIDR exhaustion: the range for pods fills up and new pods never get an address. The sign is pods stuck at creation with "no free addresses" while the nodes look idle. Size the pod CIDR for the busiest day, or add a second block, which is what custom networking is for.
  • Overlapping pod ranges: the pod CIDR is also in use by a peered network or an office, so packets for it are routed to pods instead. The sign is a destination that answers as the wrong thing, from inside the cluster only. Plan address blocks across every network you will ever connect.
  • Overlay MTU: tunnelling adds bytes to each packet, so a full-size packet no longer fits and is dropped. The sign is that small requests work and large ones hang. Lower the pod MTU to leave room for the parcel, or go VPC-native.

…but

Checkout was taking money again, and Nadia had spent the whole evening calling the endpoint by its address. The checkout pods, she realised, never called anything inside the cluster by an address at all. They called orders, and basket, and the names did not look like any DNS she had met. Ruth sent her home. "Sunday," she said. "Eleven. Bring the notebook."

The problem

At 11:00 on Sunday the call had three faces on it, then four. Jonas joined from a train, wedding suit swapped for a hoodie, and said sorry before anyone had said hello.

"You tested," said Sam. "You tested from the wrong place. Every one of us has tested from the right place for the wrong reason. Checkout's been up since 21:47. We're tidying."

Jonas let out a breath he seemed to have been holding since Saturday morning.

Nadia shared her screen. She had been reading the resolver file inside a checkout pod, the one that tells a program where to send names.

search checkout.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
nameserver 10.96.0.10
options ndots:5

Beside it she had Saturday's logs from the cluster's own DNS. For every call to Paystream there were four lookups, not one: api.paystream.example.checkout.svc.cluster.local, then the same name with svc.cluster.local, then cluster.local, each answered "no such name", and only then api.paystream.example. During the retry storm the cluster's resolver had done four times the work for every retry, and three quarters of it was for names that could never exist.

"That's a setting," said Jonas. "I can explain it."

"Let her," said Ruth.

Nadia could, mostly. By 11:40 they had agreed a list: a trailing dot on the Paystream hostname in the client's config; checkout's 60 s wait for Paystream cut to 10 s, under the load balancer's 30; retries with backoff and jitter instead of three in a row. Then, while she had the cluster open, she asked it a question she had never asked.

$ kubectl get networkpolicy -A
No resources found

"So inside the cluster," said Ruth, "anything can call anything."

"Yes."

"Write that down too."

◷Back then

Kubernetes was announced in June 2014 with a rule that every pod gets its own address, and within a week of using it, Ruth said, anyone could see the catch. Pods die. That is the point of them. A pod that crashes is replaced by a new one, on whichever node has room, with whichever address is free. Put that address in a configuration file and the file is wrong by the afternoon.

Ruth had lived the slow version of this in her data centre years: a spreadsheet of which application lived on which server and port, kept by hand, and wrong in the same way HOSTS.TXT had been wrong in 1983. The Kubernetes team's answer was there from the first releases. A Service: a name, and a stable virtual address that stood for a changing set of pods. A small program on every node, kube-proxy, kept the virtual address pointing at pods that were actually alive. A resolver inside the cluster turned the name into the virtual address, so a program could say orders and never learn a pod address at all.

Then came the question of HTTP arriving from outside. The early answer was the Ingress: one object that said "this host and this path go to that Service", and a controller, a proxy of the kind chapter 19 met, that read the object and did the routing. It worked, and then it sprawled. Each vendor's controller needed settings the object had no field for, so they went in as annotations, until a typical Ingress was three lines of routing and thirty lines of annotations that only one controller understood.

The people who looked after Kubernetes networking, SIG Network, with Tim Hockin among its longest-serving leads, spent years on a successor. Gateway API reached version 1.0 in October 2023. Its design split the roles: the people who run the cluster own the Gateway, and the people who own an application attach routes to it. Ruth said it was the sorting office again, with the pigeonholes labelled by who was allowed to touch them.

The idea

A Service is a name and a stable virtual address placed in front of a set of pods chosen by label. The pods come and go; the Service does not. In the postal picture it is a department name that never moves although the staff change desks. The virtual address is the ClusterIP, and the odd thing about it is that no interface anywhere owns it. No pod has it. No node has it. It exists only in the packet-rewriting rules on every node.

Those rules are written by kube-proxy, a program that runs on each node, watches the list of Services and the pods behind each one, and keeps the node's rules current. When a pod sends a packet to a ClusterIP, the node rewrites the destination to one live pod's real address before the packet leaves, the mirror image of the SNAT in chapter 29. The reply is rewritten back on the way in. The sending pod never learns which pod answered.

The name comes from cluster DNS, a resolver that runs inside the cluster and answers for names of the shape orders.checkout.svc.cluster.local: the Service, its namespace, and a fixed suffix. Anything else it forwards to the VPC's resolver, which is how api.paystream.example reached the private endpoint on Friday.

Short names work because of search domains: a list of suffixes the resolver tries in turn when a name is not found. A pod in the checkout namespace can say orders, and the resolver tries orders.checkout.svc.cluster.local first. The rule for when to try the suffixes is ndots: a name with fewer dots than this number is treated as short and gets the suffixes first. Kubernetes sets it to 5. api.paystream.example has two dots, so it is tried with every suffix, fails three times, and only then goes out as itself.

A trailing dot, api.paystream.example., tells the resolver the name is complete and skips the suffixes. So does a lower ndots.

For traffic arriving from outside, an Ingress is an object that says which hostnames and paths go to which Service, and an Ingress controller is the proxy that reads it and does the work; the load balancer in front sends everything to the controller. Its successor, Gateway API, describes the same thing with separate objects for the people who run the cluster and the people who own a route, and with fields for the things Ingress had to express as annotations.

Inside the cluster, the networking model means every pod can reach every pod. That is a feature until it is a finding. A NetworkPolicy is the in-cluster firewall: it selects pods by label and says which other pods, namespaces or ports may talk to them, and the CNI plug-in enforces it at each pod's interface, much as the cloud enforces a security group at each network interface (chapter 24). With no policy, nothing is enforced. With one policy that selects a pod and allows nothing, that pod is closed to everything but what later policies open. Policies select by label, not by address, which is the zero-trust shape from chapter 28, and the shape the Paystream rule should have had.

Remember it as: A Service is a name that stays while the pods move; cluster DNS gives the name, kube-proxy makes the address real.

At Kettle, every retry on Saturday had cost four lookups, and nothing in the cluster had ever stopped a pod from talking to anything else. Both were true before Friday. Friday was when anyone looked.

⚠Where it breaks
  • Pod-to-pod traffic with no NetworkPolicy attack: with no policy, a compromised storefront pod can call the orders Service, the database, or anything else by name. The tell-tale is get networkpolicy returning nothing, and no plug-in that would enforce it anyway. Start each namespace with a default-deny policy, open only the calls each Service needs, and confirm the plug-in enforces policies at all.
  • ndots lookups: external names with fewer than five dots are tried with every search suffix first, so each call costs several failed lookups. The sign is a cluster resolver busy answering "no such name", and slow first requests. Add a trailing dot, lower ndots for that pod, or cache near the node.
  • Service with no endpoints: the Service's label selector matches no pod, so the ClusterIP has nowhere to send. The sign is "connection refused" on a name that resolves fine. Compare the selector with the pods' labels before anything else.
  • Cluster DNS under a retry storm: every retry is a lookup, so the resolver becomes the next thing to fall over. The sign is lookups timing out while the application servers idle. Backoff on the client, and a cache on each node.
  • Ingress annotations that only one controller understands: routing rules written as vendor annotations work in one cluster and do nothing in another. The sign is an Ingress that "applies" cleanly and routes wrong. Gateway API gives those settings real fields.

…but

By 13:00 the list was done and Jonas's train had taken him into a tunnel, with a thumbs-up as his last message. Sam sent round the agenda for Monday's review that evening. Item three read: service mesh with mTLS (proposal). Nadia looked it up and found a courier at every desk.

Chapter 31 · Act VIIThe Mesh#

The problem

At 10:00 on Monday the small meeting room had a whiteboard, five chairs and a plate of pastries nobody had touched. Sam had the agenda. Jonas, back from the wedding and back on the platform, had item three, and had clearly spent the train journey on it.

"If we'd had a mesh with mTLS," he said, "the endpoint's rule wouldn't have mattered. Every call carries an identity. Identity, not address. Ruth said it herself on Saturday."

Ruth did not say whether she had.

Nadia had done her own homework, because she had learned over the weekend not to come to a room without a capture. Before the meeting she had run the debug pod once more, this time listening to the traffic between checkout and the orders Service, inside the cluster, where nothing had ever gone wrong.

GET /orders/8831 HTTP/1.1
Host: orders.checkout.svc.cluster.local
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs

She put it on the screen. "That's plaintext. Anyone with a pod in the cluster could read the token. There's no policy stopping them having a pod in the cluster, either. We found that yesterday."

"A mesh fixes both," said Jonas. "Every pod gets a sidecar. The sidecars talk TLS to each other with certificates the mesh hands out. Retries and timeouts become settings in one place instead of in six client libraries. We'd have seen Friday's failure in the mesh dashboard at 16:03."

It sounded right. Nadia could feel it sounding right, and could feel Ruth waiting.

"Do we need it?" said Ruth. It was not rhetorical. "How many services?"

"Six," said Sam.

"How many teams?"

"One."

Nadia wrote do we need it? in the notebook, and did not yet know the answer.

◷Back then

Ruth told this one herself, because she had been in the room for the second half of it.

In 2016 a small company called Buoyant released Linkerd. Its founders, William Morgan and Oliver Gould, had come from Twitter, where the code that handled timeouts, retries and failures between services had been written into a library that every program linked. The library worked, and every change to it meant rebuilding every program. Linkerd moved that code out of the program and into a proxy that ran beside it, and Buoyant popularised the name the pattern still carries: the service mesh.

In May 2017 Google, IBM and Lyft announced Istio. Lyft brought Envoy, a proxy it had built for its own services. Istio put one in every pod as a sidecar and added a control plane that handed each sidecar a certificate naming the workload it sat beside, so that every call between services was mutual TLS and a policy could be written once and apply everywhere. Ruth had watched the announcement from a data centre she was in the middle of emptying and thought: that is my load balancer, cut into a thousand pieces and placed next to every desk. She was not sure whether it was a compliment.

The third date is earlier. In December 2014 a change by Alexei Starovoitov went into Linux 3.18: extended BPF, eBPF, a way to load small programs into the running kernel, each checked before loading so it cannot crash the machine or loop forever, and run them at points in the network path. For years it was a tool for people who wrote packet filters. Then the mesh people noticed that much of what a sidecar did, routing, counting, enforcing policy, could be done in the kernel without a proxy per pod, and a second generation of meshes and network plug-ins grew up without sidecars at all.

Ruth's view was that each step was right, and that none of them was free.

The idea

A sidecar is a second container in the same pod, sharing the pod's network namespace (chapter 29), so it sees every packet in and out of the application without the application knowing. The application talks to what it thinks is the network; the sidecar is standing in the doorway. A service mesh is the set of all those sidecars plus a control plane that configures them: which services exist, who may call whom, how long to wait, when to retry, and which certificate each sidecar should present. The sidecars are the data plane, the control plane is the controller, the same split chapter 24 met in software-defined networks.

The security part is mTLS, mutual TLS. In the TLS of chapter 17 only the server proved who it was. In mutual TLS both sides present a certificate, and each checks the other's before a byte of the request is sent. The mesh's control plane is its own certificate authority: it issues each sidecar a short-lived certificate whose name is the workload, checkout in the checkout namespace, and renews it every few hours. Identity now travels inside the connection, not in the address it came from. A rule can say "orders accepts calls from checkout", and it holds whether checkout's pods are in 10.0, 100.64 or a cluster on another continent. That is the courier at every desk who checks both IDs before handing anything over.

The second gift is that retries and timeouts become policy. Instead of six client libraries with six opinions, the mesh holds one setting per route: wait this long, retry this many times, with this backoff, and never let retries exceed this share of traffic. A retry budget of that kind is what stops the retry storm of chapter 21 from forming. The mesh also records every call it carries, so the dashboard Jonas imagined is real: on Friday it would have shown checkout's calls to Paystream failing at 16:02, by destination, with a timeout as the reason.

Then the cost. A sidecar is a proxy, and a proxy per pod means memory and CPU in every pod, a hop added to every call, a control plane to run and upgrade, certificates that must rotate on time, and one more layer to reason about at 21:00 on a Saturday. The sidecar-less meshes built on eBPF, programs running inside the kernel on each node, move much of that work out of the pod and remove the extra hop, but the control plane, the certificates and the learning are still there.

So the question is not whether a mesh is good. It is what the alternative costs. For six services and one team, the plaintext finding is fixed by a shared client library that speaks TLS, or by a mesh. The missing policy is fixed by NetworkPolicy, which the cluster already supports. The timeouts are fixed by changing six numbers, which was Sunday's work. A mesh pays for itself when there are more services than one team can change one at a time, when several teams must agree on identity, or when a regulator wants encryption inside the cluster in writing.

Remember it as: A mesh moves the network's manners, identity, retries and timeouts, out of every program and into a proxy you run instead.

On Friday a mesh would have named the failure sooner. It would not have stopped it, because Paystream's endpoint was not in the mesh and the rule that dropped the packets was outside the cluster altogether.

⚠Where it breaks
  • Plaintext traffic inside the cluster attack: calls between pods carry tokens and customer data unencrypted, trusting that only pods are listening. The sign is a capture from any debug pod that reads like a web page. Mutual TLS between services, from a mesh or a shared library, and NetworkPolicy so that fewer pods can listen at all.
  • A mesh added before it is needed: a small team adopts a mesh for one feature and inherits a control plane, certificate rotation and an extra proxy in every pod. The sign is an outage caused by the mesh itself, debugged by the one person who understands it. Fix the specific problem first; adopt the mesh when the count of services, not the conference talk, demands it.
  • Retries stacked on retries: the client library retries, the sidecar retries, and the load balancer retries, so one failure becomes twenty-seven requests. The sign is a traffic multiplier with no matching rise in users, the Saturday morning shape. Retry in one place, with a budget.
  • Sidecar not ready: the application starts before its sidecar and its first calls fail, or the sidecar stops last and a finished job hangs. The sign is errors only in the first seconds of a pod's life. Order the start-up, and let jobs tell the sidecar when they are done.
  • Expired mesh certificates: the control plane stops renewing, every sidecar's certificate lapses at once, and every call in the cluster fails together. The sign is a cluster-wide outage with a timestamp that matches a certificate lifetime. Alert on time to expiry, not on failure.

…but

At 10:55 Sam capped his pen. The whiteboard had a question on it and no answer yet, which Ruth said was the right state for a whiteboard. "Review at eleven," he said. "The whole weekend on one board. Nadia, you start."

EpilogueThe Whole Journey#

The incident review

Monday, 11:00. The meeting room had a whiteboard that nobody had cleaned since the summer, and Sam cleaned it now, because Ruth had asked for the whole wall. Nadia stood at it with her notebook. Jonas sat near the door, back from the wedding, with the expression of a man who expected to be asked why. Nobody asked him why. Ruth had been firm about that: the review was for the system, not the people, and the first line on the whiteboard said so.

What happened

When What Chapter
Fri 15:58 Jonas merges "platform: private connectivity to payments": a private endpoint for Paystream inside the VPC, with private DNS on, to stop paying for NAT and to stop running out of NAT ports 8, 14, 27
Fri 16:02 About a third of checkouts fail with a connection timeout. Dashboards stay green 0, 1, 2
Fri 16:30–17:25 The failing hop is checkout → Paystream. The error is below HTTP. The API works from a laptop 3, 4, 5, 6
Fri 17:30 A rolling restart of checkout kills the pooled connections that were still working. Failures jump to about 80% 7, 22
Fri 17:35 A capture from a debug pod shows SYN out, nothing back: dropped, not refused 7

Fri 22:00 A silent drop smells like a firewall, but the endpoint lives in the platform account. Nadia is sent home to sleep 15
Sat 08:00–12:00 Timeouts mismatched (load balancer 30 s, checkout 60 s). Health checks green because they never come from a pod. The storefront is "up" because it is cached. The traffic spike is Kettle's own retries. The pods that still worked held HTTP/2 connections opened before 15:58 16, 17, 19, 20, 21, 22
Sat 14:00–18:00 The VPC has a second address block, 100.64.0.0/16. Flow logs on the endpoint interface show REJECT from 100.64.3.17. The security group allows 10.0.0.0/16 23, 25, 26
Sat 21:00 Pods use the secondary CIDR, and traffic that stays inside the VPC keeps the pod's address. The rule is widened to include 100.64.0.0/16. Checkout recovers at 21:47 29
Sun 11:00 Client timeouts, backoff and DNS settings tidied. NetworkPolicy noticed missing. Jonas joins the call 30
Mon 10:00 The review. A mesh is proposed; the question is whether it is needed 31

Why it happened

  1. The endpoint's security group allowed the node subnet, 10.0.0.0/16, and the cluster's pods live in 100.64.0.0/16 (chapters 26, 29).
  2. Traffic from a pod to a destination inside the VPC is not translated to the node's address, so it arrived from 100.64.x.x (chapter 29). On the old path, out through the NAT gateway, that was hidden (chapter 14).
  3. Security groups drop silently, so the symptom was a timeout, which looks like a slow server (chapters 7, 15).
  4. The change was tested from a node, where the source address was 10.0.x.x, so the test passed (chapter 29).
  5. The failure was partial and then grew, because pooled HTTP/2 connections and DNS caches aged out at different rates, and a restart removed the survivors (chapters 11, 22).
  6. Retries without backoff, from the app and from checkout, multiplied the load until it looked like an attack (chapter 21).
  7. Mismatched timeouts turned a thirty-second wait into a grey box customers could not read (chapter 16).

What changes

  • Rules that allow traffic from the cluster name the cluster's own security group, or an identity, rather than an address range. Nobody has to remember that there is a second CIDR (chapters 26, 28).
  • Connectivity changes are tested from where the traffic really comes from: a pod, not a node (chapter 29).
  • Timeouts shrink from the outside in: the client waits longer than the load balancer, the load balancer longer than checkout, checkout longer than its call to Paystream. Retries get backoff and jitter (chapters 16, 21).
  • Flow logs stay on for the endpoint subnet, and the first question in any "it times out" incident is "who dropped it?" (chapter 26).
  • Large platform changes avoid Friday afternoons, and the change ticket names what to test and from where (chapter 8).
  • NetworkPolicy goes in before the mesh does. The mesh waits until there is a second reason for it (chapters 30, 31).

Jonas said, near the end, that he had been right about the endpoint and wrong about the test, and Ruth said that was the usual ratio.

One request, end to end

This is the journey the book has been following. Each hop has a chapter.

  1. The phone opens the app, which asks for shop.kettle.example/checkout. The request is an HTTP message (16) inside a TLS session (17) inside TCP segments (7) inside IP packets (9) inside Wi-Fi frames (6).
  2. Wi-Fi and the home router carry the frames to the ISP. The router's NAT swaps the phone's private address for the household's public one (14).
  3. The ISP hands the packets to the internet, where routers forward them hop by hop using routes they learned through BGP (12, 13).
  4. DNS has already been asked, before any of that: the phone's resolver walked from the root to Kettle's authoritative servers, or answered from its cache (11). The answer pointed at the CDN.
  5. The CDN edge nearest the phone terminates TLS, serves the storefront from cache, and forwards anything dynamic, such as checkout, to Kettle's origin (20). It also absorbs floods (21).
  6. The load balancer at the edge of Kettle's VPC accepts the connection, checks the health of the targets, and forwards to one of them (19). It gives up after 30 s.
  7. The VPC routes the packet through a public subnet into a private one, past a network ACL and into a node's security group (25, 26).
  8. The node receives the packet on its network interface, and the host's virtual switch delivers it into the right network namespace (24, 29).
  9. The checkout pod handles the request and calls Paystream. The name resolves through cluster DNS, then the VPC's resolver, to the private endpoint (30, 11).
  10. The private endpoint is a network interface in the VPC. Its security group decides whether the pod's packet is allowed in. On Friday, it was not (26, 27, 29).
  11. Paystream's API answers over TLS, with a certificate for its public name (17). The reply retraces the path, and the phone shows a confirmation.

Every hop can drop, delay or rewrite what passes through it, and every hop has a different person responsible for it. That is the whole subject.

The sorting office: the metaphor in one table

Concept Metaphor
Packet / frame A letter in an envelope; the frame is the mailbag it travels in for one leg
Encapsulation / layers Envelopes inside envelopes, each office reads only its own
IP address Street address of the building
Port Flat number inside the building
MAC address The name painted on the van for one street
Subnet / CIDR A postcode district: the prefix is the district, the rest the house
ARP Shouting down the corridor "who lives at number 12?"
DHCP The council assigning a house number when you move in
Router / routing table The sorting office and its pigeonholes by postcode
Default gateway / default route "Everything else goes to the main sorting office"
BGP / autonomous system Countries' postal services agreeing which routes they will carry
DNS The phone book / directory enquiries
TCP Registered post: numbered, signed for, resent if lost
UDP A postcard: cheap, fast, no receipt
Circuit / packet switching Booking a private road for the whole trip / letters sharing every road
NAT The company post room: one public address, internal desk numbers
Firewall / security group / NACL The guard at the door with a list / a guard for each flat / a checkpoint at the district boundary that checks every crossing both ways
TLS A sealed, tamper-evident envelope with a verified return address
VPN A sealed diplomatic pouch carried through public post
Load balancer The reception desk sending visitors to any free clerk
CDN / cache Local branch offices holding copies of popular forms
DDoS A million junk letters to one address
VLAN / VPC Separate post rounds sharing one building / a gated estate you rent inside a city you don't own
Overlay network Letters inside parcels carried by another courier (and this is where the metaphor stops helping)
Private endpoint A private letterbox for an outside company, installed inside your estate
Kubernetes Service A department name that never moves although the staff change desks
Service mesh / mTLS A courier at every desk who checks both IDs before handing anything over
Zero trust Every door checks your badge, even inside the building

How we got here: three timelines

Computers were scarce, so people queued for them, then shared them through terminals, then wanted to share them across cities. The answer that won was not a better telephone call but a new idea: chop the data into packets, let every packet find its own way, and keep the network itself as dumb as possible. By 1974 the pieces existed to join networks together.

Almost everything in a modern packet was standardised in these two decades: the addresses, the transport, the names, the routing between networks, the web and its encryption. The internet also learned, the hard way, that it was not a village: a worm, congestion collapse and address exhaustion each forced a defence that we still live with.

The network moved into software and then into other people's buildings. Switches became programs, data centres became rentable slices, and the perimeter stopped meaning anything, so trust moved from addresses to identities. The protocols underneath barely changed; what changed was who runs them and how many layers of them sit between your code and the wire.

What is what: a glossary

One line each, with the chapter that explains it.

Act I

  • Sharing scarce machines (1): the reason networks exist; one expensive computer, many people who need it.
  • Batch processing (1): jobs submitted on cards and run one after another, results collected later.
  • Time-sharing (1): one machine switching between users so fast that each believes it is theirs.
  • Terminal (1): a keyboard and screen with no computer of its own, wired to one that has.
  • Modem (1): a device that turns data into sound a telephone line can carry, and back.
  • Client and server (1): the one that asks and the one that answers; a role, not a machine.
  • Circuit switching (2): reserving a path for the whole conversation, as the telephone network did.
  • Packet switching (2): cutting data into packets that share paths with everyone else's.
  • Store-and-forward (2): each node receives a whole packet, then sends it on.
  • ARPANET (3): the 1969 network that proved packet switching worked.
  • IMP (3): Interface Message Processor, the ARPANET's dedicated routing computer.
  • Host (3): a computer that runs applications, as opposed to the machines that move packets.
  • NCP (3): the ARPANET's first host-to-host protocol, replaced by TCP/IP in 1983.
  • Email (3): the first application that made people want the network.

Act II

  • Internetworking (4): joining different networks so a packet can cross all of them.
  • Gateway (4): the machine that sits between two networks and passes packets across; today called a router.
  • End-to-end principle (4): put intelligence at the ends and keep the middle simple.
  • Protocol (5): an agreed format and sequence for messages, so strangers' machines can talk.
  • Encapsulation (5): each layer wraps the layer above in its own header.
  • OSI model (5): the seven-layer reference model of 1984, still used for vocabulary.
  • TCP/IP model (5): the four layers that are actually run: link, internet, transport, application.
  • Layer 4 and layer 7 (5): transport (TCP, ports) and application (HTTP); the two layers engineers name most.
  • Ethernet (6): the standard for frames on a local wire, from Metcalfe's 1973 memo.
  • MAC address (6): the hardware address of a network interface, meaningful only on the local segment.
  • Collision (6): two senders transmitting at once on a shared wire; switches ended it.
  • Hub versus switch (6): a hub repeats to everyone; a switch learns addresses and sends to one port.
  • Frame (6): the unit of data at the link layer, carrying one packet for one hop.
  • MTU (6): the largest frame a link will carry; bigger packets must be fragmented or dropped.
  • Wi-Fi (6): Ethernet's radio cousin, with the same frames and addresses over the air.
  • TCP (7): the reliable byte stream: ordered, acknowledged, retransmitted.
  • UDP (7): single packets with no guarantees; cheap and fast.
  • Port (7): a number that picks the program inside the host; 443 is HTTPS.
  • Three-way handshake (7): SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK: how a TCP connection starts.
  • Sequence number (7): the count of bytes sent, so the receiver can order and acknowledge them.
  • Retransmission (7): sending again what was not acknowledged in time.
  • Congestion control (7): slowing down when the network drops packets, after Jacobson's 1988 fix.
  • RFC (8): Request for Comments, the document series in which internet standards live.
  • IETF (8): the engineering body that produces RFCs by rough consensus and running code.
  • Flag day (8): a cutover on which everyone must change at once; 1 January 1983 was the big one.
  • Change window (8): an agreed time for risky changes, with people awake and ready.

Act III

  • IPv4 address (9): a 32-bit number written as four parts, such as 10.20.4.31.
  • Network and host part (9): the prefix that names the network and the remainder that names the machine.
  • Address classes (9): the old fixed split into class A, B and C networks, replaced by CIDR.
  • CIDR (9): the slash notation, 10.0.0.0/16, that says how many bits are the network.
  • Subnet mask (9): the same split written as 255.255.0.0.
  • ARP (10): asking the local segment which MAC address holds an IP address.
  • DHCP (10): leasing an address, a mask, a gateway and a resolver to a machine that joins the network.
  • Default gateway (10): the router a host sends to when the destination is not local.
  • DNS (11): the distributed directory that turns names into addresses.
  • Root server (11): the top of the DNS tree, which knows who runs each top-level domain.
  • Top-level domain (11): .com, .uk, .example: the first branch below the root.
  • Authoritative server (11): the server that holds the real records for a domain.
  • Recursive resolver (11): the server that walks the tree on your behalf and caches the answers.
  • Record types (11): A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), TXT (text).
  • TTL (11): how many seconds an answer may be cached.
  • Split-horizon DNS (11): the same name answered differently inside and outside a network.
  • Router (12): the device that forwards packets between networks by looking at the destination address.
  • Routing table (12): the list of prefixes and where to send packets for each.
  • Longest-prefix match (12): the most specific route wins.
  • Default route (12): 0.0.0.0/0, the route for everything not otherwise listed.
  • Traceroute (12): discovering the hops by sending packets whose TTL expires one hop further each time.
  • OSPF (12): a protocol routers inside one organisation use to share routes.
  • Autonomous system (13): a network under one administration, with its own number.
  • BGP (13): the protocol by which autonomous systems tell each other what they can reach.
  • Peering and transit (13): exchanging traffic as equals, or paying someone to carry it.
  • Internet exchange (13): a building where many networks peer over one switch.
  • IPv4 exhaustion (14): the central pool of addresses ran out in 2011.
  • Private address ranges (14): 10/8, 172.16/12 and 192.168/16, never routed on the internet.
  • NAT (14): rewriting private addresses to a public one at the edge, and back.
  • Port translation (14): NAT's trick of using port numbers to tell inside connections apart.
  • Carrier-grade NAT (14): an ISP doing NAT for whole neighbourhoods.
  • IPv6 (14): 128-bit addresses; enough for everything, adopted slowly.

Act IV

  • Packet filter (15): a firewall that judges each packet alone by its headers.
  • Stateful firewall (15): one that remembers connections and lets replies through.
  • DMZ (15): the half-trusted zone between the internet and the inside.
  • Default deny (15): block everything, then allow what is needed.
  • Drop versus reject (15): silently discard, or send back a refusal; drops look like slowness.
  • Perimeter (15): the idea that there is an inside and an outside, and a wall between them.
  • URL (16): the address of a resource: scheme, host, path.
  • HTTP request and response (16): a method and a path, then a status code and a body.
  • Status code (16): 200, 404, 500, 504: the response's one-line verdict.
  • Header (16): a name and a value sent with a request or response.
  • Cookie (16): a value the server asks the client to send back, so it can remember you.
  • Stateless (16): each HTTP request stands alone; the server keeps no memory between them.
  • Timeout (16): how long a hop waits before giving up, and the cause of most grey boxes.
  • TLS (17): the layer that encrypts a connection and proves who the server is.
  • Certificate (17): a signed statement binding a name to a public key.
  • SNI (17): the client naming the host it wants at the start of TLS, so one address can serve many names.
  • HTTPS (17): HTTP inside TLS.
  • Leased line (18): a private circuit rented from the telephone company.
  • VPN (18): a private network carried, encrypted, across a public one.
  • IPsec (18): the 1995 standard for encrypting at the IP layer.
  • Site-to-site (18): a VPN joining two networks, as opposed to one person to a network.
  • Split tunnelling (18): sending only some traffic through the VPN.
  • Load balancer (19): the device that spreads connections over many servers and checks they are alive.
  • Round-robin (19): taking turns, the simplest way to spread load.
  • L4 versus L7 load balancing (19): balancing connections, or balancing requests after reading them.
  • Reverse proxy (19): a server that accepts requests on behalf of others and forwards them.
  • Health check (19): a periodic test that decides whether a target gets traffic.
  • Sticky session (19): sending one client to the same server each time.
  • TLS termination (19): ending the encrypted session at the balancer rather than the server.
  • Keep-alive and connection pooling (19): reusing one connection for many requests.
  • Cache (20): a copy kept close by so the original is not asked again.
  • CDN (20): a network of caches placed near users, since Akamai in 1998.
  • Edge location (20): one of the CDN's sites, where the user's connection ends.
  • Anycast (20): one address announced from many places, so you reach the nearest.
  • Cache invalidation (20): making a cache forget something that changed.
  • DoS and DDoS (21): overwhelming a service with traffic, from one source or many.
  • Rate limiting (21): refusing requests beyond an agreed rate.
  • Retry storm (21): clients retrying so hard that they become the flood.
  • HTTP/1.1 (22): persistent connections, one request at a time on each.
  • Head-of-line blocking (22): one slow response holding up everything queued behind it.
  • HTTP/2 (22): many requests in flight on one connection, since 2015.
  • Multiplexing (22): interleaving several streams on one connection.
  • QUIC (22): a transport over UDP with TLS built in, standardised in 2021.
  • HTTP/3 (22): HTTP over QUIC.
  • gRPC (22): a remote-procedure-call protocol built on HTTP/2.
  • WebSocket (22): a long-lived two-way connection that starts as an HTTP request.

Act V

  • Data centre (23): a building of racks, power and cooling, built around its network.
  • Three-tier network (23): access, aggregation and core switches, the classic data-centre shape.
  • Spanning tree (23): Perlman's 1985 protocol that stops switched networks looping.
  • VLAN (23): a virtual LAN: one switch carrying several separate networks by tagging frames.
  • Spine-leaf (23): every leaf switch connected to every spine, after Clos's 1953 design.
  • East-west traffic (23): server to server inside the data centre, now most of the traffic.
  • Virtualisation (24): running many machines as software on one physical host.
  • Virtual switch (24): the switch inside the host that connects its virtual machines.
  • Overlay network (24): a network built by carrying frames inside packets of another network.
  • VXLAN (24): the 2014 standard for Ethernet frames inside UDP packets.
  • SDN (24): software-defined networking: a program decides what switches do.

Act VI

  • VPC (25): a private, isolated network inside a public cloud.
  • Subnet, public and private (25): a slice of the VPC in one zone, with or without a route to the internet.
  • Route table (25): the routing table attached to a subnet.
  • Internet gateway (25): the VPC's door to the internet for public subnets.
  • NAT gateway (25): the managed post room that lets private subnets reach out without being reached.
  • Availability zone (25): one of several separate data centres that make up a cloud region.
  • Security group (26): a stateful allow-list attached to a network interface.
  • Network ACL (26): a stateless, ordered list applied at the subnet boundary.
  • Stateless (26): judging each packet alone, so the reply needs its own rule.
  • Flow logs (26): a record of what the VPC accepted and rejected.
  • VPC peering (27): joining two VPCs so they route to each other.
  • Transit gateway (27): a hub that many VPCs and sites connect to.
  • Private endpoint (27): a network interface in your VPC that leads privately to a service outside it.
  • Hybrid connectivity (27): VPNs and dedicated lines between the cloud and your own buildings.
  • Egress (27): traffic leaving your network, and the bill for it.
  • Segmentation (28): dividing a network so a breach of one part does not reach the rest.
  • Micro-segmentation (28): doing that per workload, not per subnet.
  • Zero trust (28): no request is trusted for where it comes from; identity is checked every time.

Act VII

  • Network namespace (29): a container's own private view of interfaces, addresses and routes.
  • veth (29): a virtual cable with one end in the container and one on the host.
  • Bridge (29): the host's software switch that veth ends plug into.
  • Kubernetes networking model (29): every pod has its own address and can reach every other without NAT.
  • CNI (29): the plug-in interface through which a cluster wires up pods.
  • Pod CIDR (29): the address range pods are drawn from; at Kettle, 100.64.0.0/16.
  • SNAT (29): rewriting the source address, done for traffic leaving the VPC and not for traffic inside it.
  • Service (30): a stable name and address in front of a changing set of pods.
  • ClusterIP (30): the Service's internal virtual address.
  • kube-proxy (30): the component that turns Service addresses into real pod addresses on each node.
  • Cluster DNS (30): the resolver inside the cluster that answers Service names.
  • ndots (30): the setting that decides how many search domains a short name is tried against.
  • Ingress (30): the older object for routing HTTP into the cluster.
  • Gateway API (30): its 2023 successor.
  • NetworkPolicy (30): the in-cluster firewall: which pods may talk to which.
  • Sidecar (31): a helper container beside the application that handles its network traffic.
  • Service mesh (31): sidecars or kernel programs on every workload, managed as one policy.
  • mTLS (31): both sides present certificates, so services prove who they are to each other.
  • eBPF (31): programs running inside the Linux kernel's network path, since 2014.

Ruth's last day

Her last day was the Friday after, which was tidy. The beige boxes in the cupboard had been labelled, photographed and written up, and the door entry system now had a diagram, which it had not had in nine years.

Nadia found her at four o'clock standing at the window with the mug, looking at the car park as though it might do something.

"Marketing has sent you a cake," Nadia said. "There's a picture of a router on it. I think they searched for 'network'."

"Does it have the word 'cloud' on it?"

"It does."

"Then it's accurate." Ruth turned round. "Did you write it up? The whole thing?"

"Thirty-two pages. Sam says nobody will read it."

"Somebody will. Somebody at two in the morning, with a timeout they can't explain. That's who you wrote it for." She picked up her bag, which had been packed since lunch. "You know what the trick was? Not the flow logs. Not the second CIDR. It was Friday, four thirty, when you couldn't tell me what checkout was. Everything after that was just finding out."

Nadia thought about the forty-one green pods, and the spinner, and the long walk from a phone to a letterbox inside an estate that Kettle rented from someone else.

"I can name it now," she said.

"Then you can debug it," said Ruth, and went to find the cake.
